question: What are the most common reasons prospects hesitate to buy?
correct_reason: Five of the six themes are supported and none is contradicted. Only the licensing and usage model concern is missing.

verdicts.reason: The answer names price as a hesitation, citing budget limits, but it doesn't give any of the specific company examples.
The answer says prospects compare OrbitFlow to cheaper tools they already have, and cites Microsoft winning on cost per seat and expanding Gainsight.
The answer covers integration and technical-fit worries, including on-premise systems that can't be exposed to the internet.
The answer covers procurement, security and compliance gates, and cites the BAA.
The answer doesn't mention worries about the seat, licensing or usage-overage model.
The answer covers maintenance burden and dependence on engineering, and cites the over-buying risk and that maintenance costs are underestimated.

[00:49] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [pause] That's a fair read of our website.
[00:53] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You're agreeing?
[00:55] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Our marketing is aimed at companies with a governance function. You don't have one, so it isn't aimed at you.
[01:04] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): So why are you calling?
[01:06] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Because our marketing being aimed at somebody else doesn't mean the product is wrong for you. But I'd want to establish that in about four minutes rather than argue with your conclusion.
[01:19] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Go on then. Four minutes.
[01:22] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What are you trying to do with Tray?
[01:25] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Order-to-deployment. A customer orders a robot cell, and then there's engineering config, procurement of the long-lead parts, build scheduling, factory acceptance testing, shipping, and site commissioning. Seven stages, five systems, and about four months elapsed.
[01:47] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And what goes wrong?
[01:49] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Nothing goes wrong exactly. Things just take longer than they should because stage four doesn't know stage three finished until someone mentions it in a meeting.
[02:01] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How much of the four months is waiting?
[02:04] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] I don't know. That's part of why we're doing this.
[02:10] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Okay. How's the Tray evaluation going?
[02:14] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Well. Genuinely well. Their team's been good.
[02:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then I'd say two things. First, I'm not going to tell you Tray is bad. It isn't. We lose to them and we beat them and it usually comes down to fit rather than quality.
[02:32] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): What's the second?
[02:34] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Three weeks in, with a decision coming, I'd be the third horse in a two-horse race, and that's usually a waste of everyone's time.
[02:44] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You're talking yourself out of it again.
[02:47] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'm being realistic about it. Unless there's something in your evaluation that isn't going well, in which case I'd want to know what.
[02:57] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] There is one thing.
[03:00] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[03:02] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Our ERP. It's a mid-market system, quite niche in manufacturing. Tray don't have a connector and we're looking at building against its API, which our one back-end developer estimates at three weeks.
[03:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Do you believe the estimate?
[03:21] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [laughs] No.
[03:23] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Nobody ever does.
[03:25] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): It'll be six.
[03:27] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd want to be honest — there's a good chance we don't have a connector either. What's the system?
[03:34] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): I'd rather not say on a cold call, if that's alright.
[03:39] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Completely fine. Then let me answer it generally. If it's a mid-market manufacturing ERP, we probably don't have a native connector, and you'd be building against the API with our generic REST action. Which is the same three weeks. Or six.
[03:57] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): So no advantage.
[04:00] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No advantage on that specific point, no. There might be one on what happens afterwards — who maintains it, whether it's reusable across the seven stages — but that's a subtler argument and I'm not going to pretend it's decisive.
[04:17] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You keep doing this.
[04:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Doing what?
[04:21] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Conceding things.
[04:23] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather concede the things that are true and be believed on the things that aren't.
[04:29] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] Alright. What's the argument you would make?
[04:35] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Honestly, only one, and it's small. You said your one back-end developer would build the ERP integration. What happens when he's busy and someone in operations wants to change which stage triggers a notification?
[04:52] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): It waits.
[04:54] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): For how long?
[04:56] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] Depends. Weeks.
[04:59] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then the question for your evaluation — for either vendor — is whether the people who own the process can change the process without him. That's testable in a week and most evaluations don't test it.
[05:15] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): How would you test it?
[05:17] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Have someone in operations, not your developer, build one real workflow. Not with the developer sitting next to them. And see what happens.
[05:29] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] That's a good test.
[05:33] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the test that predicts whether you're happy in two years. Run it against Tray — I mean that, run it against Tray, you're three weeks in and it costs you nothing.
[05:46] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): And if they pass?
[05:48] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then buy Tray. You'll have made a good decision for a good reason.
[05:54] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [laughs] You are the strangest salesperson I've spoken to this year.
[05:59] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll take that.
[06:01] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Look — I'm not going to restart the evaluation. We've got a decision date and I'm not moving it.
[06:09] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I wouldn't ask you to.
[06:11] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): But I'll do this. Send me something short — not a deck — on how you'd approach the seven-stage thing, and specifically on the operations-can-change-it question. If we go with Tray and it doesn't work out, I'll know who to call.
[06:29] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather have that than a demo you sit through politely.
[06:34] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): When's the decision?
[06:36] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Mid-October. Fourteenth, I think, or thereabouts.
[06:42] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Would it be worth a thirty-minute call before mid-October? Not a pitch. I'd walk through how I'd structure the seven stages and you can use the thinking whichever vendor you pick.
[06:56] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You'd do that knowing we'll probably go with Tray?
[07:01] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You're a hundred and fifty people building robots. You'll be four hundred people in three years and you'll be buying something else. I'd rather be the person who was useful.
[07:14] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] That's a long game.
[07:17] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the only game in a market this small.
[07:21] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Alright. Send the note. If it's good I'll do the thirty minutes.
[07:27] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask one thing before you go?
[07:30] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Go on.
[07:32] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The four months. Have you got a number for what a month costs you?
[07:37] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): A month of delay on a cell? Roughly, we recognise revenue on commissioning, so — a month is a month of revenue on a two hundred thousand pound order.
[07:50] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And how many orders in flight?
[07:53] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Eleven at the moment.
[07:55] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then if instrumenting the seven stages tells you where two weeks are going, that's a much bigger number than either vendor's licence.
[08:05] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] That's the slide I need for my board, isn't it.
[08:10] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the slide you need regardless of who you buy from.
[08:14] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [laughs] Send the note, Leo.
[08:17] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I will. Thanks Rafael.
[08:20] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Bye.

answer.summary: Prospects most often hesitate for five reasons: price, procurement/security gates, uncertainty about integration/technical fit, fear of implementation or maintenance burden, and doubts about ROI versus existing tools. A recurring theme is that they want proof on their own workflows first, not a generic demo or headline quote. These are prospect-side objections and caveats; OrbitFlow reps often acknowledge them and sometimes even steer toward a smaller pilot or architecture session instead.

claims.statement: Price is a common hesitation, with multiple prospects saying the starting price is higher than their budget or hard limit.

citations.speaker: Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow)
citations.quote: Growth starts at eighteen hundred a month, that's up to thirty users, annual agreement.

citations.speaker: Imogen Price (COO, Fable Media)
citations.quote: I know. That's the problem. I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand.

citations.speaker: Yvonne Deeks (Practice Operations Manager, Trafford Dental Group)
citations.quote: The price is the real problem, by the way. Even if you'd been brilliant.

claims.statement: Procurement, legal, security, and compliance gates commonly slow or block deals.

citations.speaker: Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust)
citations.quote: For services, it varies. Practically, anything meaningful goes through a framework or a tender

claims.statement: Integration and technical fit worries are frequent, especially whether OrbitFlow can connect to the customer's systems or work with their architecture.

citations.quote: We have systems that will not be exposed to the public internet.

citations.speaker: Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow)
citations.quote: We do not have a native concept of a matter-level ethical wall that reads your barrier definitions

citations.speaker: Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics)
citations.quote: Our ERP. It's a mid-market system, quite niche in manufacturing.

claims.statement: Prospects often worry that the workflow would be harder to maintain or change than it looks, and that the real owner would still need engineering help.

citations.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying

citations.speaker: Marcus Chen (VP Business Operations, Juniper Cloud Tools)
citations.quote: Maintenance and observability are the real costs and Ava consistently underestimates them.

citations.speaker: Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow)
citations.quote: What happens when he's busy and someone in operations wants to change which stage triggers a notification?

claims.statement: Many prospects want evidence that the workflow produces real ROI, and some explicitly compare OrbitFlow to cheaper existing tools or doing nothing.

citations.speaker: Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch)
citations.quote: I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.

citations.speaker: Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow)
citations.quote: If the decision is purely cost per seat, Microsoft wins and everyone knows it.

citations.speaker: Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning)
citations.quote: Which is why I want the model to be honest. If the answer is "expand Gainsight, it's cheaper," I want to be able to say that.

claims.statement: Prospects repeatedly ask to validate the claim on their own actual process before buying, often preferring instrumentation, an architecture session, or a recorded example over a generic demo.

citations.quote: One representative workflow working with real enough data.

citations.speaker: Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services)
citations.quote: I'd rather have a roadmap and architecture conversation than a commercial proposal at this point.

citations.speaker: Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow)
citations.quote: The first phase of something like this shouldn't be automating the voids process.

PROSPECT: Acme Logistics
INDUSTRY: Logistics
COMPANY SIZE: 650 employees
STAGE: Discovery / first demo
DURATION: 30 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow

[05:31] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I can probably still justify it if we replace enough manual work, and maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for. But I'd need a clearer ROI story than "it saves time."

That's what the deck says. In practice EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions. So a single workflow diagram on a slide is a bit misleading.
[06:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's really useful.
[06:21] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): The process people describe and the process people run are not always the same thing.
[06:28] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): They're never the same thing.
[06:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Okay. Let me play the stack back to make sure I've got it. Salesforce, Slack, Snowflake, Gainsight, Google Sheets.
[06:42] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's the core, yeah.
[06:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which one's the system of record for the process?

[07:09] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): We also have Workato. I don't want you to think we've got nothing.
[...]
[07:33] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): So I don't want to frame this as "we have no automation." The question is whether a different layer gives us better maintainability and operational control.
[07:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a much better framing than most people give us, honestly. And to be clear, we're not trying to replace every integration platform. Plenty of our customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep systems integration and use us for the business-owned workflows — the ones with human decisions, exceptions, cross-functional handoffs.
[08:09] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's closer to how we'd think about it. I'd be nervous if the proposal was migrate everything.
[08:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It won't be.
[08:19] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I'm more interested in a bounded set of workflows where the current approach is visibly failing.
[08:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Okay, so let me try one. Is that the right shape?
[08:47] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's the right shape. One caveat though, and it's a big one. The happy path is not the hard part. Anyone can demo the happy path.
[...]
[13:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): We cache metadata but refresh it, and mapping errors surface on the run. question: What concerns did customers raise about pricing?
correct_reason: This is a broad question. Five of the six required cores are supported and none is contradicted. Only the Fable Media 10-user request is missing.

verdicts.reason: The answer says the 1,800/month Growth price is too high for small teams. It cites the Trafford Dental 200-300/month budget (CALL-019) and the Zapier comparison of about 2,000 a year against roughly 19,000 (CALL-015). It does not mention Cedar & Finch's 800-1,000 expectation.
The answer cites Cedar & Finch's 15,000 sign-off limit against 21,600 a year and Fable Media's 20,000 limit, above which the founder approves.
A full bullet covers the fear that occasional approvers will need full seats. It cites CALL-002, 007, 009 and 010, which likely map to BrightPath, Greenline and Inkwell, among others.
The answer cites Ember's worry about unpredictable usage overages as volumes grow. It does not cover Juniper's subflow question, and the Lumen overage evidence is too vague to count.
The answer never mentions Fable Media asking for 10 users or monthly billing.
The answer cites CALL-004 asking for transparency on professional services and premium connectors.

=== CALL-001 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-001
DATE: 2026-06-03

[04:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Okay. Look, I'm going to jump ahead slightly because I'd rather you hear this early than at minute fifty-five —

[05:06] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Hm.
[05:08] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a "hm".
[05:11] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): It's more than I expected. And I know why — I'd mentally benchmarked this against Zapier, which is not a fair comparison, but that's the number that was in my head.
[05:24] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's a very common anchor. It's also the wrong one, but I'd rather earn that than assert it.
[05:31] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I can probably still justify it if we replace enough manual work, and maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for. But I'd need a clearer ROI story than "it saves time."
[05:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Understood. Let's come back to that properly later — I don't want to give you a number before I know your user model, because that's exactly where proposals become misleading.
[...]
[09:00] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I want to see what happens when data's missing. When an API times out. When an approver does nothing for two days. When the account changes state halfway through the workflow.
[...]
[12:02] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): How technical is this actually? Because every vendor says no-code right up until you hit the one thing the connector doesn't do.
[...]
[13:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): We cache metadata but refresh it, and mapping errors surface on the run. For high-impact flows I'd genuinely recommend explicit validation at the start rather than assuming every source field is populated. And you can alert when error rates cross a threshold.
[13:23] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I'd want that in the evaluation. A demo with clean data proves nothing to me.
[...]
[14:19] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): One thing I noted from your pre-call form — you've got roughly a hundred and forty customer-facing users but you'd only expect twenty-five to actually build or administer workflows?
[...]
[15:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You'd mentioned AI in your notes. I'll be brief on it because I don't think it's the centre of gravity here. We treat it as optional steps inside a workflow rather than making the whole product autonomous. Classification, summarisation, extracting fields from text, drafting something for a human to approve.
[15:27] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Good. I'm wary of the word agent, mostly because it usually means nobody can explain why something happened.
[...]
[16:11] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes to both. AI steps are explicit, inspectable steps. Admins can restrict which models are allowed. Enterprise customers can disable AI features outright. We log the model configuration used for a run. And we don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
[16:33] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That last one needs to be in writing. Not in a demo.
[...]
[18:04] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Who can see the payload? We'll have workflows where an admin should know a step failed without necessarily seeing all the customer data in it.
[...]
[19:40] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): It is, relatively. We need the usual vendor review, SSO, audit logs. We don't have a special data-residency requirement for this project.
[19:52] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That is a shorter list than most.
[19:55] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): We're not healthcare. But we will ask for screenshots or documentation, not just yes/no answers on a questionnaire.
[20:05] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's fine. Baseline is SOC 2 Type II. SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise. Encryption in transit and at rest. Audit logs cover administrative and workflow events. Retention configurable within supported ranges. EU residency available on Enterprise if you ever need it.
[...]
[20:35] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yes, all of that under the normal process, and we can complete your questionnaire. One ask from me — if anything on your list is an absolute gate, flag it now. I'd rather not spend six weeks on a pilot that can't pass review.
[20:52] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): The gating issue isn't security for us.
[...]
[21:34] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): One thing I'd add — what happens to data sent to an LLM provider is a question you'll get from your security team, and the honest answer is it depends on configuration and provider. We use enterprise API arrangements where available, we document subprocessors. If your policy is strict, AI can be disabled, or we scope the pilot to deterministic steps while security reviews model usage separately.
[...]
[22:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Right — pricing properly. What counts as a user, since you asked.
[22:17] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Yes, because we may have a small number of builders and a lot of people who only approve something or receive a notification.
[22:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Builders and full workspace users are the licensed users. Approval-only or notification-only can be structured differently depending on the package. I'm deliberately not giving you an exact number today because without the user model any number I give you is misleading.
[22:46] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Please make that explicit in the proposal. I do not want to find out in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
[22:56] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It'll be itemised — assumed builder count, viewer and approver population, expected workflow volume, and any one-time services separately.
[23:07] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Thank you.
[23:10] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): On ROI — is this headcount avoidance, cycle time, error reduction, engineering maintenance?
[23:18] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I would not sell this internally as headcount reduction. It wouldn't survive contact with my CFO and it's also not true. The stronger case is consistency and speed. We've got expensive people doing coordination work because the systems don't carry enough process context.
[23:38] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): And there's an engineering cost nobody sees. A script takes two days to write and then quietly eats a few hours every month forever. That never makes it into the original estimate.

question: Which competitors were mentioned, and in what context?
correct_reason: The answer supports every required competitor core, and none is contradicted.

verdicts.reason: Workato is named as the incumbent, and the answer mentions expanding the existing Workato contract. It leaves out the Verity churn and why Workato won that deal.
The answer covers the bake-off against a Tray PoC that has run for six weeks and the three-week Tray evaluation. It does not say Kestrel crossed OrbitFlow off its list.
Zapier is cited in CALL-003 (Cedar & Finch), CALL-006 (Fable, 'good enough') and CALL-015 (Oakhill, 'should never have left'). Acme's price anchor and Lumen are not mentioned.

Power Automate is described as embedded or bundled through the Microsoft agreement in several calls, including the claims triage call. The specific accounts are not named, so only the Pinewood claims-triage detail is clearly covered.
MuleSoft is described as the integration backbone DeltaWorks owns. The answer does not say that a business-workflow layer built on it is the cheaper alternative.
The answer covers Make for branching, expanding Gainsight, and Retool Workflows or Step Functions for an internal build.

PROSPECT: Acme Logistics

PARTICIPANTS:

TRANSCRIPT
[07:17] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): The data team uses it for a handful of back-office integrations. It works. But RevOps finds it too technical, and Rachel doesn't want every workflow change to become an IT ticket.
[...]
[20:58] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor. That's the conversation I'll have to win internally. I'd rather you knew that upfront than designed around an assumption.
[21:16] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I appreciate that, genuinely. We'll write it up as a pilot exit criterion. If we can't satisfy it, that should be an explicit result, not something that surfaces in procurement at the end.
[21:31] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's a good answer.
[21:34] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): One thing I'd add — what happens to data sent to an LLM provider is a question you'll get from your security team, and the honest answer is it depends on configuration and provider. We use enterprise API arrangements where available, we document subprocessors. If your policy is strict, AI can be disabled, or we scope the pilot to deterministic steps while security reviews model usage separately.
[22:03] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): That separation would help. AI's interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation case over.
[22:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Right — pricing properly. What counts as a user, since you asked.
[22:17] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Yes, because we may have a small number of builders and a lot of people who only approve something or receive a notification.
[...]
[25:29] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): One representative workflow working with real enough data. Security gates understood. A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises. And the people who'll operate it have to believe they can own it — that last one is not a small thing.
[25:48] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): And the honest comparison is Workato, or just improving what we already have. Not doing nothing.
[25:57] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Agreed. We can define the pilot against the status quo and the alternative. And a perfectly valid outcome is "don't buy OrbitFlow" if the existing approach meets the criteria more cheaply.
[26:11] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): You're allowed to say that?
[26:13] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather say it now than in month nine.
[26:17] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Fair enough. Look — my read is I'm interested enough to test it. If you can give us a sandbox I can supply three real workflows and we'll see whether the exception handling is as good as it looked today.
[26:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's exactly what I'd want. So — we send the security pack and a short architecture summary, you send the representative workflow and sample data, and we jointly write three to five pilot success criteria. Then we decide on the sandbox.

[...]

[18:19] Ava Sinclair (Staff Software Engineer, Juniper Cloud Tools): We have EU customers and a data residency commitment in some contracts. So EU residency is probably the requirement.
[...]
[18:53] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's scoped on the Salesforce side by the permissions of the user or integration account you connect with. We use what you give us. We don't have a separate layer that further restricts it.

The answer says not every step is manual and the problem is the gaps between automated pieces.

context.text:
=== CALL-001 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-001
DATE: 2026-06-03
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Acme Logistics
INDUSTRY: Logistics
COMPANY SIZE: 650 employees
STAGE: Discovery / first demo
DURATION: 30 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Jon Bell, Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow
- Rachel Morgan, VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics
- Tom Alvarez, Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Morning. Can you hear me okay? I think my headset decided today was the day.
[00:06] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): You're fine. Bit quiet but fine.
[00:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Great. So, um, Tom's dialling in a few minutes late, he's got something running over. Shall we start and catch him up?
[00:19] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Yeah, let's not waste the hour.
[00:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Okay. So before we get into it — I actually spent three years at a freight forwarder before I moved into software. Middle office, mostly. So when your team said "we run onboarding out of a spreadsheet" I did have a bit of a flashback.
[00:41] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): [laughs] Which spreadsheet?
[00:44] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Ours was called MASTER_FINAL_v7. There was no v6. Nobody ever found out what happened to v6.
[00:52] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's — honestly that's not far off. Ours has tabs colour-coded by whoever last panicked.
[01:01] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Right. Okay, so my plan for today, roughly — I want to spend the first chunk just understanding how you actually handle this, and then Jon can show the parts of the product that map onto that. Not the full tour. I'd rather skip the bits that aren't relevant.
[01:18] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Please. I've sat through the full tour from three vendors this quarter.
[01:24] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Understood. So — where does it hurt?
[01:29] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): The short version is we've got too much operational work living between systems. And I want to be clear up front, we're not looking for another dashboard. We've got dashboards. We need something that actually moves work along and makes it visible who owns what.
[01:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can you give me a concrete one?
[01:51] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Sure. Handoffs between sales, onboarding and customer success. All of that is managed through spreadsheets and Slack reminders. So renewal risks and implementation blockers get noticed late. Not never — late.
[02:09] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How late is late?
[02:12] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Depends. Sometimes a week. Sometimes we find out at the QBR, which is — yeah.
[02:20] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And is it that the steps are manual, or —
[02:23] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): No, and this is the thing people get wrong. It's not that every step is manual. We have automation in places. The problem is the gaps between the automated pieces. Something runs, then nothing happens for four days, then a human notices.
[02:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the pattern we see most, actually. Connecting systems is one problem. Operating the process that sits on top of the connections is a different problem, and the second one is usually where the pain is.
[02:56] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Yeah.
[02:58] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Do you have numbers on it, or is it anecdotal?
[03:03] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Mix. We've got outcome metrics. The operational telemetry is weak. We can usually tell you something was late after the fact. We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed, or whether the same thing happened fifteen times last month.
[03:24] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That last one is the one that costs you.
[03:27] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's the one that costs us, yes.
[03:32] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): — sorry, sorry, I'm here. Sorry. Was on with a customer.
[03:37] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No problem at all. We were just on current state.
[03:41] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Right. Well, my angle is slightly different from Rachel's. I want to make sure we don't buy a tool that looks great in a demo and then becomes another thing my team has to babysit. We've already got automation nobody quite owns.
[03:57] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Say more on that.
[04:00] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): When things work, nobody notices. When something sticks, the escalation path depends entirely on who happens to see it. And people compensate — they build their own reminders, their own little spreadsheets, someone wrote a script once. And then that person leaves.
[04:20] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): We have at least two scripts running that I could not tell you the author of.
[04:26] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Three.
[04:27] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Three. Great. [crosstalk]
[04:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Okay. Look, I'm going to jump ahead slightly because I'd rather you hear this early than at minute fifty-five —
[04:38] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Actually, can I do that? Because I have the same instinct. What does this cost? Roughly. I don't need a quote, I need to know whether we're in the same postcode.
[04:50] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Fair. Growth starts at eighteen hundred a month, that's up to thirty users, annual agreement. Enterprise is custom — that's where the governance and security capabilities sit, plus higher usage.
[05:06] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Hm.
[05:08] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a "hm".
[05:11] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): It's more than I expected. And I know why — I'd mentally benchmarked this against Zapier, which is not a fair comparison, but that's the number that was in my head.
[05:24] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's a very common anchor. It's also the wrong one, but I'd rather earn that than assert it.
[05:31] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I can probably still justify it if we replace enough manual work, and maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for. But I'd need a clearer ROI story than "it saves time."
[05:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Understood. Let's come back to that properly later — I don't want to give you a number before I know your user model, because that's exactly where proposals become misleading.
[05:57] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can I correct something, actually — sorry, on the process thing. Earlier we described onboarding as standardised. That's what the deck says. In practice EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions. So a single workflow diagram on a slide is a bit misleading.
[06:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's really useful.
[06:21] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): The process people describe and the process people run are not always the same thing.
[06:28] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): They're never the same thing.
[06:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Okay. Let me play the stack back to make sure I've got it. Salesforce, Slack, Snowflake, Gainsight, Google Sheets.
[06:42] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's the core, yeah.
[06:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which one's the system of record for the process?
[06:49] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Depends on the object. Customer and commercial data, that's clear. Tasks and tickets, that's somewhere else. And then a lot of the actual context is in chat, which is — that's the problem, isn't it. That's why a workflow layer is even interesting to us.
[07:09] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): We also have Workato. I don't want you to think we've got nothing.
[07:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Tell me how it's used.
[07:17] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): The data team uses it for a handful of back-office integrations. It works. But RevOps finds it too technical, and Rachel doesn't want every workflow change to become an IT ticket.
[07:31] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I really don't.
[07:33] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): So I don't want to frame this as "we have no automation." The question is whether a different layer gives us better maintainability and operational control.
[07:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a much better framing than most people give us, honestly. And to be clear, we're not trying to replace every integration platform. Plenty of our customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep systems integration and use us for the business-owned workflows — the ones with human decisions, exceptions, cross-functional handoffs.
[08:09] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's closer to how we'd think about it. I'd be nervous if the proposal was migrate everything.
[08:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It won't be.
[08:19] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I'm more interested in a bounded set of workflows where the current approach is visibly failing.
[08:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Okay, so let me try one. If we picked a single workflow for phase one — opportunity closes in Salesforce, create the onboarding plan, assign tasks based on product mix, notify the right Slack channel, escalate stalled milestones up to CS leadership. Is that the right shape?
[08:47] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's the right shape. One caveat though, and it's a big one. The happy path is not the hard part. Anyone can demo the happy path.
[08:58] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[09:00] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I want to see what happens when data's missing. When an API times out. When an approver does nothing for two days. When the account changes state halfway through the workflow.
[09:14] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's — sorry, Maya, can I —
[09:16] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yeah, go.
[09:18] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's exactly the right level to test at, and it's the bit I'd want you to push on. Workflows are event-driven but each run holds state. So you can branch on data, pause for approvals, retry external actions, set timeout rules, and push an exception into a queue rather than just failing quietly.
[09:40] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can the queue be owned by a team? Not a named person. People change roles constantly here and individual ownership is genuinely one of the reasons our current stuff breaks.
[09:53] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes. Route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. And the run history persists, so an admin can see the inputs, which steps ran, where it stopped.
[10:08] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Okay. That's better than what we've got.
[10:12] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): There's a second use case I'd flag, not for phase one — identifying renewal risk by combining CRM fields, support activity and product usage signals out of Snowflake. I don't need it now. I do want to know the architecture doesn't rule it out.
[10:31] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It doesn't. Different shape of workflow — that's more scheduled and query-driven than event-driven — but same platform.
[10:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Jon, do you want to show them rather than describe it?
[10:45] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yeah. Let me share. [pause] Bear with me, it's — sorry, Teams is asking me for permission again.
[10:56] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Take your time.
[11:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): There we go. Can you see the builder?
[11:07] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): We can see your inbox.
[11:09] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Ah. Yep. Sorry. [pause] Now?
[11:16] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Yes.
[11:18] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Right. So left-hand side is triggers and actions, middle is the flow, right-hand panel is the config for whatever step you've selected. A workflow can start from a SaaS event, a schedule, a webhook, a database query, or another workflow.
[11:36] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'll start this one from a record-change event, check a few required fields, enrich from a second system, then branch. And the thing I'd draw your attention to is that we push people towards small reusable components. You really don't want a single two-hundred-step workflow. You want subflows — account lookup, approval, notification, incident creation.
[12:02] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): How technical is this actually? Because every vendor says no-code right up until you hit the one thing the connector doesn't do.
[12:12] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yeah, that's fair criticism and I'm not going to pretend. Simple mapping and branching is visual. Transformations use expressions. On Enterprise you can package reusable JavaScript steps if you need to. There's a generic REST action and webhooks. We don't claim every workflow is no-code. What we aim for is that the workflow stays understandable even if an engineer supplied one custom component.
[12:41] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's a better answer than pretending my team will never touch code. I care about reducing dependency, not eliminating engineers.
[12:52] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Schema changes though. We've had integrations die because someone renamed a field or added a picklist value, and the automation just — didn't say anything.
[13:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): We cache metadata but refresh it, and mapping errors surface on the run. For high-impact flows I'd genuinely recommend explicit validation at the start rather than assuming every source field is populated. And you can alert when error rates cross a threshold.
[13:23] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I'd want that in the evaluation. A demo with clean data proves nothing to me.
[13:30] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Agreed. Give us dirty data.
[13:34] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): On integrations — you'd said Salesforce is mandatory, Slack and Snowflake matter for phase one, Gainsight would be useful but isn't essential. Which one's the deal-breaker?
[13:48] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): The system of record. If that connector's unreliable, none of the rest matters. After that it's the collaboration and data systems, because that's where context goes missing.
[14:02] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): For your stack it's a mix of native connectors and API-based options. What I'd want to do in a pilot is validate each required operation rather than just point at a logo on our integrations page.
[14:17] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Good.
[14:19] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): One thing I noted from your pre-call form — you've got roughly a hundred and forty customer-facing users but you'd only expect twenty-five to actually build or administer workflows?
[14:31] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's about right. Maybe thirty at a stretch.
[14:36] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Okay, that matters for the commercial model. Maya will come back to it.
[14:41] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): [dog barking] Sorry — sorry, one second. [pause] Sorry, that's me, ignore that.
[14:52] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Not a problem. Ours is worse, honestly, I have a cat who sits on the keyboard during forecast calls.
[15:01] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): [laughs] Right, sorry, carry on.
[15:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You'd mentioned AI in your notes. I'll be brief on it because I don't think it's the centre of gravity here. We treat it as optional steps inside a workflow rather than making the whole product autonomous. Classification, summarisation, extracting fields from text, drafting something for a human to approve.
[15:27] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Good. I'm wary of the word agent, mostly because it usually means nobody can explain why something happened.
[15:36] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a reasonable prior.
[15:39] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Where would you use a model versus just rules?
[15:43] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Rules for anything already structured and safety-critical. Model where the input is genuinely unstructured or the task is semantic. Summarising a long ticket thread, fine. Deciding whether to issue a refund above a threshold — that should stay deterministic and permissioned.
[16:03] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can we see the prompt and the model config? And can we switch AI off entirely for a workspace?
[16:11] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes to both. AI steps are explicit, inspectable steps. Admins can restrict which models are allowed. Enterprise customers can disable AI features outright. We log the model configuration used for a run. And we don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
[16:33] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That last one needs to be in writing. Not in a demo.
[16:38] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Noted, and agreed — that belongs in the contract, not on a call.
[16:44] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can the thing refuse to answer if the source material is thin? The failure mode I dislike is a very confident summary built on one incomplete note.
[16:56] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You can design for that. Require a minimum set of fields or sources before the AI step runs, ask the model to return structured confidence, route low-confidence cases to review. I wouldn't sell you model confidence as a mathematical guarantee though. The better control is usually evidence plus workflow policy.
[17:19] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): For anything customer-facing or exec-facing I'd want a link back to the underlying records. People need to be able to challenge the output.
[17:30] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's how we think about it in production too — not just "did the model answer", but did it use the right records, were the key facts preserved, did the uncertain cases get escalated.
[17:45] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Let me show you run history, actually, because it's related. [pause] So — filter by workflow, status, time, or a business field. Open a run, you get every step, inputs, outputs, timing, retries, any human approval.
[18:04] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Who can see the payload? We'll have workflows where an admin should know a step failed without necessarily seeing all the customer data in it.
[18:15] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Permissions can separate workflow administration from business viewing. I'd flag that exact field-level masking requirements should be part of security design rather than something I promise now. We do support role-based access, workspace separation, and secrets aren't displayed in run logs.
[18:36] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Can we get metrics out into our own monitoring? I don't want operationally critical automation only visible inside a vendor console.
[18:47] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Run events and metrics through APIs and webhooks, and audit export on Enterprise. Several customers forward failures into their incident tooling. Happy to show actual payloads in a technical session.
[18:59] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): That matters to me a lot more than a nice dashboard.
[19:04] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Version history — if someone changes a condition on a Friday afternoon and it breaks, can we see exactly what changed?
[19:13] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Version history and change metadata, yes. Rollback and promotion patterns vary a bit by workflow and package. For your evaluation I'd actually suggest we include a change-management scenario rather than just building the thing once.
[19:30] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Yes. That's closer to real life.
[19:35] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Let's do security, and I suspect this one's quick for you.
[19:40] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): It is, relatively. We need the usual vendor review, SSO, audit logs. We don't have a special data-residency requirement for this project.
[19:52] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That is a shorter list than most.
[19:55] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): We're not healthcare. But we will ask for screenshots or documentation, not just yes/no answers on a questionnaire.
[20:05] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's fine. Baseline is SOC 2 Type II. SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise. Encryption in transit and at rest. Audit logs cover administrative and workflow events. Retention configurable within supported ranges. EU residency available on Enterprise if you ever need it.
[20:27] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can you send the SOC 2 report, subprocessor list, DPA, architecture diagram, retention documentation?
[20:35] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yes, all of that under the normal process, and we can complete your questionnaire. One ask from me — if anything on your list is an absolute gate, flag it now. I'd rather not spend six weeks on a pilot that can't pass review.
[20:52] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): The gating issue isn't security for us.
[20:56] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[20:58] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor. That's the conversation I'll have to win internally. I'd rather you knew that upfront than designed around an assumption.
[21:16] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I appreciate that, genuinely. We'll write it up as a pilot exit criterion. If we can't satisfy it, that should be an explicit result, not something that surfaces in procurement at the end.
[21:31] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's a good answer.
[21:34] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): One thing I'd add — what happens to data sent to an LLM provider is a question you'll get from your security team, and the honest answer is it depends on configuration and provider. We use enterprise API arrangements where available, we document subprocessors. If your policy is strict, AI can be disabled, or we scope the pilot to deterministic steps while security reviews model usage separately.
[22:03] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): That separation would help. AI's interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation case over.
[22:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Right — pricing properly. What counts as a user, since you asked.
[22:17] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Yes, because we may have a small number of builders and a lot of people who only approve something or receive a notification.
[22:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Builders and full workspace users are the licensed users. Approval-only or notification-only can be structured differently depending on the package. I'm deliberately not giving you an exact number today because without the user model any number I give you is misleading.
[22:46] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Please make that explicit in the proposal. I do not want to find out in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
[22:56] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It'll be itemised — assumed builder count, viewer and approver population, expected workflow volume, and any one-time services separately.
[23:07] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Thank you.
[23:10] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): On ROI — is this headcount avoidance, cycle time, error reduction, engineering maintenance?
[23:18] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I would not sell this internally as headcount reduction. It wouldn't survive contact with my CFO and it's also not true. The stronger case is consistency and speed. We've got expensive people doing coordination work because the systems don't carry enough process context.
[23:38] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): And there's an engineering cost nobody sees. A script takes two days to write and then quietly eats a few hours every month forever. That never makes it into the original estimate.
[23:52] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): For a pilot we can baseline one or two things before we automate — elapsed time, number of manual touches, exception rate, engineer hours spent maintaining the current process.
[24:06] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I'd add adoption. A technically correct workflow that everyone routes around is a failed implementation.
[24:15] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): And edge cases, not average time. The pain is always in the weird ten percent.
[24:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Who owns it day to day if this works?
[24:26] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I own the project. IT security and the VP of Customer Success sign off. Finance gets involved above twenty-five thousand a year, so — yes, finance gets involved. Operationally I'd expect a small central group owning standards, business teams contributing requirements.
[24:47] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): With naming conventions. And change control on the important ones. And a rule that somebody other than the creator can understand each production flow.
[24:58] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's more or less our recommended model. Start with a few centrally owned templates, define who can publish to production, separate dev from prod.
[25:10] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Timing — you'd said choose a vendor before end of July, first workflows live in September?
[25:18] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's the intent. It'll slip. It always slips. But that's the plan.
[25:24] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What has to be true to move from evaluation to decision?
[25:29] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): One representative workflow working with real enough data. Security gates understood. A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises. And the people who'll operate it have to believe they can own it — that last one is not a small thing.
[25:48] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): And the honest comparison is Workato, or just improving what we already have. Not doing nothing.
[25:57] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Agreed. We can define the pilot against the status quo and the alternative. And a perfectly valid outcome is "don't buy OrbitFlow" if the existing approach meets the criteria more cheaply.
[26:11] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): You're allowed to say that?
[26:13] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather say it now than in month nine.
[26:17] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Fair enough. Look — my read is I'm interested enough to test it. If you can give us a sandbox I can supply three real workflows and we'll see whether the exception handling is as good as it looked today.
[26:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's exactly what I'd want. So — we send the security pack and a short architecture summary, you send the representative workflow and sample data, and we jointly write three to five pilot success criteria. Then we decide on the sandbox.
[26:52] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Quick ones before we drop, if there's time?
[26:56] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go.
[26:58] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can workflows call our internal APIs without us exposing them publicly?
[27:03] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): If they're publicly reachable, outbound calls are trivial. For private networks it depends on your environment and may need an agent or a controlled gateway. I'd want to validate that rather than assume.
[27:18] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can secrets be rotated without editing every workflow?
[27:22] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes. Connections and credentials are centrally managed and referenced. Rotation happens at the connection layer.
[27:31] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Can a human modify data before approving? Sometimes approval isn't just yes or no.
[27:38] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Approval forms can collect structured inputs and those values feed subsequent steps. For heavily customised forms some customers use their own front end and call us through the API.
[27:52] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Last one. Can we trigger a workflow manually for a one-off exception?
[27:58] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes, permissions allowing. It's useful during migration and for exception recovery.
[28:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Let me summarise what I heard, and correct me. You don't need automation for its own sake. The opportunity is making a small number of cross-system processes observable, easier to change, and less dependent on specific individuals. The pilot has to prove integration reliability, exception handling, governance, and that there's a credible operating model on your side.
[28:31] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Yes. And keep the first workflow narrow. I'd rather have one thing we trust than six demos.
[28:39] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can you also write down the assumptions you made today? Some of what we told you was approximate and I don't want it hardening into requirements by accident.
[28:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Will do. Written recap with open questions separated from confirmed requirements.
[28:58] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Great. Send it over and we'll come back with sample inputs. Thanks both.
[29:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Thanks.
[29:06] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thanks. And Tom — good luck with the dog.
[29:10] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): [laughs] Cheers.

answer.summary: Acme Logistics said their current workflow is fragmented across spreadsheets, Slack, Salesforce, Snowflake, Gainsight, Google Sheets, and Workato, with work and context spread between systems rather than in one process layer. They said the biggest problems are gaps between automated steps, late visibility into handoffs and blockers, and overdependence on specific people or scripts. They also said the process is not fully standardized in practice: EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions, and they want the first workflow kept narrow and limited to a small set of cross-system processes.

correct_reason: Ember is correctly ranked at the top and the answer clearly frames the ranking as an inference. However, it moves Juniper out of the top tier, misses the Workato condition for Acme, and puts gated prospects (BrightPath, DeltaWorks) among the strongest.

verdicts.reason: The answer ranks Ember (CALL-005) as the strongest prospect and mentions the six-week pilot and sandbox request. It does not mention Tray's head start or the remediation deadline.

The summary puts Juniper in the 'more conditional or slower-moving' group, not the top tier. It does mention the four-week evaluation with a September go/no-go and that Marcus wants this, but it says nothing about the in-house build option.
The answer mentions the three real workflows in a sandbox. It never says the deal depends on whether Acme expands Workato instead, and it ranks Acme as a strong buyer.
The answer calls Inkwell a 'strong conditional prospect' tied to the backward analysis and cites the late-September decision.
The answer says plainly: 'This is an inference from the calls, not a commitment by any prospect.'

PER-CALL FINDINGS (each call was read on its own for this question; quotes verified)
CALL-001 (Acme Logistics): Acme Logistics looks like a reasonably strong prospect, but not a done deal. Rachel and Tom both show real interest and agree to a pilot/sandbox next step, while explicitly flagging Workato and internal commercial review as potential blockers.
   [08:19] Rachel Morgan: "I'm more interested in a bounded set of workflows where the current approach is visibly failing."
   [20:58] Rachel Morgan: "The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor."

   [26:17] Rachel Morgan: "my read is I'm interested enough to test it. If you can give us a sandbox I can supply three real workflows"
   [28:31] Rachel Morgan: "Yes. And keep the first workflow narrow. I'd rather have one thing we trust than six demos."
   [28:58] Rachel Morgan: "Great. Send it over and we'll come back with sample inputs."
CALL-002 (BrightPath Health): BrightPath Health looks like a real potential buyer, but only conditionally: Priya is open to a limited pilot and sees the workflow/backlog problem as compelling, while Elliot is supportive if security and least-privilege requirements are satisfied. This is not a firm purchase signal yet because they repeatedly say the BAA/security answer is the gate and broader deployment is a separate decision.
   [29:50] Priya Shah: "My read is I would still consider a limited pilot with synthetic or clearly non-PHI data."
   [28:53] Priya Shah: "One representative workflow working with real enough data. The security gates understood, and by understood I mean answered."

[27:19] Ava Sinclair (Staff Software Engineer, Juniper Cloud Tools): I can give you an order of magnitude. It'll be a guess.
[27:24] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): A labelled guess is fine. What I won't do is put an unlabelled guess in a proposal and let it look like a commitment.
[27:33] Marcus Chen (VP Business Operations, Juniper Cloud Tools): What counts as a user, incidentally?
[27:36] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Builders and full workspace users are the licensed ones. Approval-only or notification-only populations can be structured differently by package. For you it's probably a small number either way.
[27:50] Marcus Chen (VP Business Operations, Juniper Cloud Tools): Ten builders, maybe. Thirty people who'd see a task.
[27:55] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then that's a straightforward shape and I'll model it explicitly.
[28:00] Ava Sinclair (Staff Software Engineer, Juniper Cloud Tools): One more technical thing before we go.
[28:03] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Go.
[28:05] Ava Sinclair (Staff Software Engineer, Juniper Cloud Tools): Idempotency. If a workflow retries a step that writes to Salesforce, do I get two records?
[28:13] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): If the downstream system isn't idempotent and the write succeeded but the response was lost, then yes, potentially. Each run keeps state and retries are visible in the run record, so you can see that it happened. But we can't make a non-idempotent API idempotent.

question: Why did customers who left decide to leave?
correct_reason: The main churn reasons for both customers are right, but two required facts are missing: Verity's minimal onboarding and the fact that Oakhill had no smaller plan available.

verdicts.reason: The answer says operations never built anything and quotes 'paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool.'
The answer names Workato as the winner because of its better core-banking connector and stronger engineering-facing story.
The two-day onboarding, its attendance figures and the declined January sessions are not mentioned.
The answer gives Growth at 1,800 a month for 30 users with only 4 people logging in, and mentions eleven workflows' worth of value.
The answer gives the move to Zapier at about 2-2.5k a year, says the product worked, and says approval forms and run history aren't worth 19k a year.
The answer only implies it through the 'five or six hundred a month' quote. It never says no smaller plan existed and does not mention the missing CSM.
