context.text:
PER-CALL FINDINGS (each call was read on its own for this question; quotes verified)
CALL-014 (Verity Payments): Only partly: they left mainly because OrbitFlow never achieved the promised business-user adoption, so the product became an engineering-owned tool with too much custom integration work for the price. Connector gaps and a stronger Workato evaluation reinforced the decision, but they said the connector gap was not the real root cause.
   [01:33] Sarah Lindqvist: "February was when we tried to build the settlement reconciliation workflow and couldn't."
   [02:41] Kwame Boateng: "The connector gap was real. But it wasn't why we left. It was the thing we pointed at."
   [02:52] Kwame Boateng: "Nobody in operations ever built anything."
   [03:21] Kwame Boateng: "So we paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool."
   [03:45] Kwame Boateng: "My operations people are good at operations. They're not good at that, and expecting them to become good at it in their spare time was naive."
   [06:19] Sarah Lindqvist: "Because we were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose main selling point was that we wouldn't have to maintain custom integrations."
   [06:19] Sarah Lindqvist: "And because the licence cost was being justified by a benefit — business-user autonomy — that wasn't materialising."
   [07:37] Sarah Lindqvist: "Two things. Their connector for our core banking platform is genuinely better than yours."
   [07:49] Sarah Lindqvist: "And their engineering-facing story is stronger."
   [12:35] Sarah Lindqvist: "They put a solutions architect on it for three days and built us a working custom connector as part of the evaluation."
   [12:49] Sarah Lindqvist: "That's when it was over, if you want the specific moment."
CALL-015 (Oakhill Property): They left mainly because OrbitFlow was more expensive than the value Oakhill could realistically use: they bought a larger plan for a future that never happened, only a few people used it, and a much cheaper alternative covered most of their needs. They also saw the approval forms and run history as the only real value, but not worth the annual cost at their size.
   [00:43] Hazel Wren: "We bought something we didn't need. That's the whole answer."
   [01:12] Hazel Wren: "We were on Growth, at eighteen hundred a month, for thirty users, when we had four people who ever logged in."
   [02:02] Hazel Wren: "About two thousand a year. Maybe two and a half with the tier we need."
   [02:14] Hazel Wren: "No. We'll lose the approval steps and we'll lose the run history"
   [03:12] Hazel Wren: "They're the three things that matter and they're worth something. They're not worth nineteen thousand pounds a year"
   [05:27] Hazel Wren: "We paid for eleven workflows' worth of value and a plan for forty."
   [07:10] Hazel Wren: "Nothing changed. That's the thing. It kept working. But the pain it solved stopped being fresh, and the invoice kept arriving"
   [12:22] Hazel Wren: "With the approval forms, yes. Without them, no, because that's the bit Zapier can't do"

=== CALL-014 (call kind: churn)
CALL ID: CALL-014
DATE: 2026-09-18
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
CUSTOMER: Verity Payments
INDUSTRY: Payments
COMPANY SIZE: 800 employees
STAGE: Churn post-mortem
DURATION: 21 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Ruth Adeyemi, Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow
- Kwame Boateng, Head of Operations, Verity Payments
- Sarah Lindqvist, Engineering Manager, Verity Payments
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Kwame, Sarah — thank you for doing this. You didn't have to.
[00:05] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): We nearly didn't, if I'm honest.
[00:08] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I know. And I want to set expectations: this isn't a save attempt. You've signed with Workato, the decision's made, and I'm not going to spend twenty minutes trying to reopen it.
[00:22] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [pause] Good. That was my concern.
[00:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What I want is to understand what went wrong properly, because two years is a long time to get something wrong and I'd like to not do it again.
[00:37] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): We'll be honest then.
[00:39] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please be.
[00:41] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I'd add — I took over this account in January, so about eight months ago. Some of what went wrong predates me and some of it doesn't, and I'd rather you told me which is which.
[00:55] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Alright. Where do you want to start?
[00:59] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): With the decision. When did you actually decide?
[01:04] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Properly? June.
[01:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): June.
[01:09] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Though I'd say the decision became inevitable in about February and it took us until June to admit it.
[01:17] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): February.
[01:19] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): February.
[01:21] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's a month after I took the account.
[01:24] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): It's not about you. I want to be clear about that.
[01:29] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I'd still like to know what happened in February.
[01:33] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): February was when we tried to build the settlement reconciliation workflow and couldn't.
[01:40] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Couldn't, or found it hard?
[01:43] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Couldn't, in the sense that the effort exceeded the value by a factor I couldn't justify to my team.
[01:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Tell me about it specifically.
[01:54] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Our settlement provider is a mid-sized European processor. You don't have a connector for them. Nobody does, to be fair — Workato doesn't either.
[02:06] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So what was the difference?
[02:09] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): The difference is that we ended up writing a custom integration either way, and once you've accepted you're writing custom integrations, you start asking what the platform is actually giving you.
[02:24] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And what was the answer?
[02:26] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Orchestration and run history, which are genuinely good. But not enough on their own for what we were paying.
[02:35] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): And this is where I'd push back on Sarah slightly.
[02:39] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Go on.
[02:41] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): The connector gap was real. But it wasn't why we left. It was the thing we pointed at.
[02:49] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What was the real reason?
[02:52] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Nobody in operations ever built anything.
[02:56] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] Say more.
[02:59] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): The entire pitch — and this is the pitch I bought, so I'm implicating myself — was that my team would own their own workflows. That we'd stop queuing behind engineering. Two years in, every single production workflow was built by Sarah's team.
[03:19] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Every one.
[03:21] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [crosstalk] So we paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. And as an engineering tool it's fine but it's not worth the premium.
[03:34] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Why didn't your team build?
[03:37] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [pause] A few reasons and none of them are flattering.
[03:42] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather have unflattering.
[03:45] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): The first workflow anyone builds is hard. Not conceptually hard — fiddly. You have to understand connections, you have to understand how data moves between steps, you have to understand what happens when something's null. My operations people are good at operations. They're not good at that, and expecting them to become good at it in their spare time was naive.
[04:11] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Did you have enablement?
[04:13] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): We had a two-day onboarding at the start. Eight people attended. Six of them never touched it again.
[04:22] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): And after that?
[04:24] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Nothing, until you arrived in January and offered some sessions.
[04:29] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Which you declined.
[04:31] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Which I declined, because by January I'd already half-concluded it wasn't going to work and I didn't want to spend my team's time on it.
[04:41] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] That's useful and it's painful.
[04:46] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): You asked.
[04:48] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I did ask. What would have changed it? If I'd arrived in month three rather than month twenty?
[04:56] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Honestly, I think if someone had sat with two of my people for a week in the first quarter and got them to ship something real, we'd still be a customer.
[05:08] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): I agree with that.
[05:10] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Not a training course. Sitting with them. Building the actual thing they needed.
[05:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): We do offer that.
[05:19] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Do you? Nobody ever offered it to me.
[05:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [pause] It's a paid professional services engagement.
[05:28] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Ah.
[05:30] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which is possibly the problem. If the thing that makes the product succeed is a paid add-on, and the customer doesn't know they need it until it's too late —
[05:41] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Then you've designed a product that fails by default for people like me.
[05:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a harsher way of putting it than I would have, but I can't argue with it.
[05:53] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Can I add the engineering perspective? Because it's different.
[05:58] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please.
[06:00] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): My team quite liked it. The run history is genuinely better than what we'd have built. The exception queues are good. When something failed at three in the morning, we could see why, and that's not nothing.
[06:16] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): So why did you support leaving?
[06:19] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Because we were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose main selling point was that we wouldn't have to maintain custom integrations. And because the licence cost was being justified by a benefit — business-user autonomy — that wasn't materialising.
[06:39] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Say the other thing.
[06:41] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): [pause] And because two of my engineers wanted to build it in-house and I spent eighteen months arguing against them, and eventually I ran out of arguments.
[06:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What was your last argument?
[06:56] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Maintenance. It's always maintenance. And it's a good argument right up until the platform also requires maintenance, at which point you're comparing two maintenance burdens and one of them costs a hundred thousand a year.
[07:13] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is that what you're paying Workato?
[07:16] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Less. Not dramatically less.
[07:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So it isn't a price decision.
[07:22] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): It's partly a price decision, because at the margin we could justify one and not the other. But no, it's not primarily price.
[07:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then what tipped it to Workato specifically?
[07:37] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Two things. Their connector for our core banking platform is genuinely better than yours. That one's just true.
[07:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It is true. We know.
[07:49] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): And their engineering-facing story is stronger. Recipes as code, better CI story, our engineers had opinions about it and the opinions were positive.
[08:02] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): So you've bought an engineering tool.
[08:05] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): [pause] Yes. That's fair. We've bought an engineering tool and stopped pretending.
[08:12] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Which is the honest conclusion. My team is never going to build workflows. That was my ambition and it was wrong, and rather than keep paying for the ambition I've accepted the reality.
[08:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask — do you think that ambition was wrong in principle, or wrong for Verity?
[08:33] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [pause] For Verity. I've seen it work elsewhere. I was at a retailer before this where the operations team genuinely did build their own things.
[08:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What was different?
[08:47] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): There was a person whose job it was. Not a champion, not an enthusiast — a role, with a title, whose entire job was building and maintaining automations for the business. Half a headcount, maybe.
[09:04] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): We never had that.
[09:06] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): We never had that and I never asked for it, because I thought the product removed the need for it.
[09:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's — I want to write that down properly, because I think it's the most important thing you've said.
[09:21] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Which part?
[09:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That the product doesn't remove the need for the role. It changes what the role has to be good at.
[09:31] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Yes. That's exactly it.
[09:34] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): We do say that, in fairness. It's in the operating model guidance.
[09:40] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Is it? I've never seen the operating model guidance.
[09:44] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] Then we don't say it, do we.
[09:48] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [laughs] Not effectively.
[09:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Let me ask about the sales process, since I ran it. What did I get wrong?
[09:58] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): You want honesty on this too?
[10:01] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Especially on this.
[10:03] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): You sold to my enthusiasm rather than to my capability. I was excited, I said my team would own it, and nobody in your organisation asked "who specifically, and what else is on their plate?"
[10:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a fair criticism.
[10:22] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): It's not that you lied. You just believed me, and you shouldn't have, because I didn't know what I was agreeing to.
[10:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I've started asking that question, for what it's worth. Not because of you — I don't want to claim that. But it's in my discovery now. "Name the person who'll build the second workflow."
[10:45] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): That's a good question. I wouldn't have had an answer.
[10:50] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the point of it.
[10:52] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Can I raise the support thing? Since we're doing grievances.
[10:57] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Go ahead.
[11:00] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): The support was inconsistent. Some tickets came back in an hour with someone who clearly understood the product. Others came back in a day with a link to documentation I'd already read and cited in the ticket.
[11:16] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's a known problem and it's a triage problem rather than a capability problem.
[11:23] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): I assumed as much. It's not why we left. But it contributed to a general feeling that we were a small account.
[11:33] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Were you treated as a small account?
[11:36] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): [pause] Probably accurately, yes.
[11:40] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's the answer, isn't it. You were an eighty-thousand-pound account in a book of accounts where that's below median.
[11:50] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): I'd worked that out.
[11:52] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Most customers do.
[11:55] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is there anything we could have done in the last six months? Genuinely, not rhetorically.
[12:02] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [pause] Probably not. By March we'd started the Workato evaluation and once that starts it has its own momentum. People invest in it, they want to be right.
[12:16] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): There was a moment in April.
[12:19] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Was there?
[12:21] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): When the Workato PoC hit the same connector problem we'd hit with you. For about two weeks it looked like we'd have the same issue either way.

answer.summary: Both customers left mainly because the product’s economics and promised use case no longer fit how they were actually using it. Verity Payments concluded OrbitFlow had become an engineering tool with custom integrations and business-user autonomy never materializing; Oakhill Property decided they were overpaying for a larger plan than they needed, with only a few useful features and a much cheaper alternative available. In both calls, the customers also pointed to a mismatch between what was sold and what their teams could realistically do, and both said some form of better fit or smaller pricing could have changed the outcome.

=== CALL-020 (call kind: cold_call)
CALL ID: CALL-020
DATE: 2026-09-30
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Kestrel Robotics
INDUSTRY: Industrial robotics
COMPANY SIZE: 150 employees
STAGE: Cold call
DURATION: 8 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Leo Grant, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Rafael Santos, COO, Kestrel Robotics
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Rafael.
[00:02] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Rafael, hi. Leo Grant, OrbitFlow. Cold call — I'll be quick and you can hang up.
[00:09] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] OrbitFlow. That's funny.
[00:13] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is it?
[00:15] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): We're three weeks into evaluating Tray.io. Your name came up on a list and got crossed off.
[00:23] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Crossed off by whom?
[00:25] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Me. About a month ago.
[00:28] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask why? Genuinely — I'm not going to argue, I just want to know.
[00:34] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Your website. It's very enterprise. Governance, compliance, workspace separation. We're a hundred and fifty people building robots. I looked at it and thought, that's not for us.
[00:49] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [pause] That's a fair read of our website.
[00:53] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You're agreeing?
[00:55] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Our marketing is aimed at companies with a governance function. You don't have one, so it isn't aimed at you.
[01:04] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): So why are you calling?
[01:06] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Because our marketing being aimed at somebody else doesn't mean the product is wrong for you. But I'd want to establish that in about four minutes rather than argue with your conclusion.
[01:19] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Go on then. Four minutes.
[01:22] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What are you trying to do with Tray?
[01:25] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Order-to-deployment. A customer orders a robot cell, and then there's engineering config, procurement of the long-lead parts, build scheduling, factory acceptance testing, shipping, and site commissioning. Seven stages, five systems, and about four months elapsed.
[01:47] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And what goes wrong?
[01:49] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Nothing goes wrong exactly. Things just take longer than they should because stage four doesn't know stage three finished until someone mentions it in a meeting.
[02:01] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How much of the four months is waiting?
[02:04] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] I don't know. That's part of why we're doing this.
[02:10] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Okay. How's the Tray evaluation going?
[02:14] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Well. Genuinely well. Their team's been good.
[02:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then I'd say two things. First, I'm not going to tell you Tray is bad. It isn't. We lose to them and we beat them and it usually comes down to fit rather than quality.
[02:32] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): What's the second?
[02:34] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Three weeks in, with a decision coming, I'd be the third horse in a two-horse race, and that's usually a waste of everyone's time.
[02:44] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You're talking yourself out of it again.
[02:47] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'm being realistic about it. Unless there's something in your evaluation that isn't going well, in which case I'd want to know what.
[02:57] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] There is one thing.
[03:00] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[03:02] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Our ERP. It's a mid-market system, quite niche in manufacturing. Tray don't have a connector and we're looking at building against its API, which our one back-end developer estimates at three weeks.
[03:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Do you believe the estimate?
[03:21] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [laughs] No.
[03:23] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Nobody ever does.
[03:25] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): It'll be six.
[03:27] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd want to be honest — there's a good chance we don't have a connector either. What's the system?
[03:34] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): I'd rather not say on a cold call, if that's alright.
[03:39] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Completely fine. Then let me answer it generally. If it's a mid-market manufacturing ERP, we probably don't have a native connector, and you'd be building against the API with our generic REST action. Which is the same three weeks. Or six.
[03:57] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): So no advantage.
[04:00] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No advantage on that specific point, no. There might be one on what happens afterwards — who maintains it, whether it's reusable across the seven stages — but that's a subtler argument and I'm not going to pretend it's decisive.
[04:17] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You keep doing this.
[04:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Doing what?
[04:21] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Conceding things.
[04:23] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather concede the things that are true and be believed on the things that aren't.
[04:29] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] Alright. What's the argument you would make?
[04:35] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Honestly, only one, and it's small. You said your one back-end developer would build the ERP integration. What happens when he's busy and someone in operations wants to change which stage triggers a notification?
[04:52] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): It waits.
[04:54] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): For how long?
[04:56] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] Depends. Weeks.
[04:59] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then the question for your evaluation — for either vendor — is whether the people who own the process can change the process without him. That's testable in a week and most evaluations don't test it.
[05:15] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): How would you test it?
[05:17] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Have someone in operations, not your developer, build one real workflow. Not with the developer sitting next to them. And see what happens.
[05:29] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] That's a good test.
[05:33] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the test that predicts whether you're happy in two years. Run it against Tray — I mean that, run it against Tray, you're three weeks in and it costs you nothing.
[05:46] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): And if they pass?
[05:48] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then buy Tray. You'll have made a good decision for a good reason.
[05:54] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [laughs] You are the strangest salesperson I've spoken to this year.
[05:59] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll take that.
[06:01] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Look — I'm not going to restart the evaluation. We've got a decision date and I'm not moving it.
[06:09] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I wouldn't ask you to.
[06:11] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): But I'll do this. Send me something short — not a deck — on how you'd approach the seven-stage thing, and specifically on the operations-can-change-it question. If we go with Tray and it doesn't work out, I'll know who to call.
[06:29] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather have that than a demo you sit through politely.
[06:34] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): When's the decision?
[06:36] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Mid-October. Fourteenth, I think, or thereabouts.
[06:42] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Would it be worth a thirty-minute call before mid-October? Not a pitch. I'd walk through how I'd structure the seven stages and you can use the thinking whichever vendor you pick.
[06:56] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You'd do that knowing we'll probably go with Tray?
[07:01] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You're a hundred and fifty people building robots. You'll be four hundred people in three years and you'll be buying something else. I'd rather be the person who was useful.
[07:14] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] That's a long game.
[07:17] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the only game in a market this small.
[07:21] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Alright. Send the note. If it's good I'll do the thirty minutes.
[07:27] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask one thing before you go?
[07:30] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Go on.
[07:32] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The four months. Have you got a number for what a month costs you?
[07:37] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): A month of delay on a cell? Roughly, we recognise revenue on commissioning, so — a month is a month of revenue on a two hundred thousand pound order.
[07:50] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And how many orders in flight?
[07:53] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Eleven at the moment.
[07:55] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then if instrumenting the seven stages tells you where two weeks are going, that's a much bigger number than either vendor's licence.
[08:05] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] That's the slide I need for my board, isn't it.
[08:10] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the slide you need regardless of who you buy from.
[08:14] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [laughs] Send the note, Leo.
[08:17] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I will. Thanks Rafael.
[08:20] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Bye.

answer.summary: Renewals are handled as account reviews first and sales conversations second: OrbitFlow’s team starts from usage, outcomes, overages, support issues, governance gaps, and the renewal deadline, then builds a proposal with line-item changes and options such as shorter terms or re-implementation. New business calls start with discovery and qualification of the prospect’s actual process, constraints, and stakeholders, often explicitly avoiding a full demo or premature pricing until the fit, architecture, or procurement gates are understood. Across both, the team is candid about limits and tends to push the next step toward a concrete test or written proposal, but renewals are more about proving continued value while new business is more about proving the problem and the fit.

Names the shared pattern: being specific about the prospect's actual process and pain, and a short, low-commitment next step that was not a generic demo.
Calls CALL-019 the outlier, but gives none of the reasons (wrong facts, no questions, leading with price).

result.question: Which cold calls produced a follow-up, and what did the successful ones have in common?

context.text:
PER-CALL FINDINGS (each call was read on its own for this question; quotes verified)
CALL-016 (Quarry Ridge Foods): This call did produce a follow-up, but only a limited one: Maya secured permission to send a single email in February, with no further calls this year and only if it’s specifically relevant to Power Automate. It was not a meeting or an open-ended next step; the follow-up was conditional and low-commitment.
   [01:54] Maya Chen: "I'll send one email in February with something specific about Power Automate"
   [02:12] Dermot Kelly: "February's fine. One email."
   [01:32] Dermot Kelly: "we've got Power Automate through our Microsoft deal, so it'd have to be pretty compelling."
   [01:54] Maya Chen: "If it's useful, reply. If it isn't, don't, and I'll leave it there."
CALL-017 (Silverline Travel): Yes — this call produced a clear follow-up, but it was conditional: Martine asked for a short page, and said a meeting would go on the diary only if the page was good. What made it work was the specific, business-relevant framing around Silverline’s actual disruption process, not a generic "workflow automation" pitch, plus respecting her time.
   [01:31] Chloe Barnes: "If you say "workflow automation" she'll be polite for a minute and then get off. If you say something about our actual business she'll listen."
   [04:42] Martine Duval: "It's handled badly. It's handled by a very good team working very hard, which is not the same as handled."
   [05:04] Martine Duval: "Alright — send me something. Not a deck. Something short that describes what you'd actually look at."
   [05:28] Martine Duval: "Send me the page and copy Chloe. If the page is good she'll put it in the diary."
CALL-018 (Beacon Housing Trust): Yes — this cold call produced a real follow-up. It ended with a concrete next step: Maya would send technical requirements, Ade would send framework information, Priya would join, and they set a week to meet. The call worked because it stayed specific and practical: real operational pain, clear technical/procurement constraints, and a jointly defined next conversation rather than a vague promise.
   [07:47] Maya Chen: "Half an hour, in the next couple of weeks, with you and whoever owns the housing management system technically."
   [08:15] Ade Balogun: "Our technical person is Priya Menon — she's our applications manager."
   [09:33] Ade Balogun: "I'll send you a list. There are three we use routinely."
   [09:55] Ade Balogun: "Alright. Send me the technical requirements, I'll send you the frameworks, and I'll get Priya. Week of the sixth?"
CALL-019 (Trafford Dental Group): This call did not produce a real follow-up. The only next step offered was to send information, but the prospect explicitly said she wouldn’t read it and preferred not to be followed up, so there was no meaningful continuation booked.
   [04:18] Alastair McCrae: "is it worth me sending you some information, just so you've got it?"
   [04:27] Yvonne Deeks: "You can send it. I'll be honest with you, I won't read it."
   [04:35] Yvonne Deeks: "I'd rather tell you that than have you follow up four times."
CALL-020 (Kestrel Robotics): Yes — this cold call produced a follow-up, but it was conditional and somewhat loose. Rafael agreed to receive a short note first, and said that if it was good, he’d do a 30-minute call before mid-October.
   [06:11] Rafael Santos: "Send me something short — not a deck — on how you'd approach the seven-stage thing"
   [06:11] Rafael Santos: "If we go with Tray and it doesn't work out, I'll know who to call."
   [06:42] Leo Grant: "Would it be worth a thirty-minute call before mid-October?"
   [07:21] Rafael Santos: "Alright. Send the note. If it's good I'll do the thirty minutes."

TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Chloe Barnes (Executive Assistant, Silverline Travel): Good afternoon, Silverline Travel.
[00:03] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Afternoon. Could I speak to Martine Duval, please?
[00:07] Chloe Barnes (Executive Assistant, Silverline Travel): Can I ask who's calling?
[00:09] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Leo Grant, from OrbitFlow. And I'll save you the next question — she isn't expecting me.

[00:27] Chloe Barnes (Executive Assistant, Silverline Travel): It sounds like the last three.
[00:30] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd imagine. Can I ask you something instead, since you're the person who'd know?
[00:36] Chloe Barnes (Executive Assistant, Silverline Travel): Depends what it is.
[00:38] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is Martine the right person for operational process problems, or is that somebody else? Because if I've got the wrong name I'd rather find out from you than waste her time.

[01:05] Chloe Barnes (Executive Assistant, Silverline Travel): Honestly? Probably. Thursday or Friday.

[01:48] Chloe Barnes (Executive Assistant, Silverline Travel): Hold on, actually — she's just come off her call. Do you want me to see if she's free?
[01:56] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): If you think it's a good moment. I'm happy to wait for Thursday if it isn't.

[03:52] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Then I'll be quicker. We work with customer operations teams where a booking or a case has to move through several systems and several people, and the failure mode is that nothing's actually broken — it's just sitting somewhere and nobody knows.
[04:11] Martine Duval (Director of Customer Operations, Silverline Travel): [pause] Go on.

=== CALL-018 (call kind: cold_call)
CALL ID: CALL-018
DATE: 2026-09-25
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Beacon Housing Trust
INDUSTRY: Social housing
COMPANY SIZE: 1,900 employees
STAGE: Cold call
DURATION: 10 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Ade Balogun, Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): Ade Balogun.
[00:02] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Ade, hi — my name's Maya Chen, I'm from a company called OrbitFlow. This is a cold call, so I'll give you the thirty-second version and you can tell me to go away.
[00:14] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): [laughs] That's refreshing. Go on.
[00:18] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): We do workflow automation, but the specific problem we're usually brought in for is cross-team processes where the work is technically visible in a system somewhere but nobody actually owns moving it along. So things sit, and you find out late.
[00:36] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): [pause] That's most of my job, actually.
[00:40] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is it? Tell me more.
[00:43] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): Well — I'm head of business change at a housing association. Everything I do is cross-team processes that nobody owns.
[00:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Give me one.
[00:55] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): Voids. Empty property turnaround.
[00:59] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I don't know that world. Walk me through it?
[01:03] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): A tenant moves out. We need to inspect the property, decide what work's needed, get the work done, do a compliance check — gas, electrical, fire — and then re-let it. Every day that property is empty costs us rent we don't collect.
[01:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What's your average?
[01:24] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): Twenty-six days. The sector benchmark for good is around eighteen.
[01:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And what's the twenty-six made of?
[01:34] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): [pause] That's exactly the question I can't answer, and it's the reason this call is going better than you expected.
[01:43] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll take it.
[01:45] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): We know the total. We know some of the stages. But when I ask why a specific property took forty-one days, the answer takes someone two hours of digging and usually ends with "it was waiting for the electrical certificate."
[02:02] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And you can't tell whether that's one property or a pattern.
[02:07] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): We cannot tell whether it's one property or a pattern. I've been asking for that for two years.
[02:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What have you tried?
[02:16] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): A dashboard. Which tells me the average is twenty-six days. Which I already knew.
[02:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] That's the most common answer I get.
[02:27] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): Is it?
[02:29] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Almost universally. People buy visibility and discover they had visibility, they just didn't have coordination.
[02:38] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): That's a good way of putting it. Can I write that down?
[02:42] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's not mine, a customer said it to me in July.
[02:47] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): [laughs] Well, tell them thank you.
[02:50] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask what systems are involved? Roughly, I don't need detail.
[02:56] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): Our housing management system, which is the big one. A repairs system that's separate. A compliance system that's separate again. And then a great deal of email and, God help us, some spreadsheets.
[03:12] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And do those three systems talk?
[03:15] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): The housing management system and the repairs system have an integration that works about eighty percent of the time. Compliance is entirely manual.
[03:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So the compliance certificate that held up your forty-one-day property —
[03:32] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): Was somebody emailing a contractor and waiting.
[03:36] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Right.
[03:38] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): You can see why I said the call was going well.
[03:42] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I can. Let me be straightforward about a few things though, because I'd rather do that now.
[03:49] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): Please.
[03:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): First — I don't know your housing management system. There's a reasonable chance we don't have a native connector for it, and we'd be working through an API or building something. That's not a dealbreaker but it's real work and it costs money.
[04:08] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): I'd assumed that. Nobody has connectors for our sector.
[04:13] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Second — you're a housing association, which means procurement.
[04:19] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): [laughs] It means procurement, yes.
[04:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Are you on a framework?
[04:24] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): We'd typically buy through one, yes. Anything over a threshold has to go through a compliant route.
[04:32] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What's the threshold?
[04:34] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): For services, it varies. Practically, anything meaningful goes through a framework or a tender, and a tender is nine months of my life.
[04:46] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then that's something we should establish early rather than in month four. I'd want to know which frameworks you use and whether we're on any of them, and if we're not, whether there's a compliant route at all.
[05:01] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): You're raising the procurement problem yourself.
[05:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather find out in week one that we can't be bought than in month six.
[05:11] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): That's — yes. Most vendors discover procurement in month six and are then very surprised about it.
[05:20] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I've been surprised about it.
[05:23] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): Everyone has.
[05:25] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Third thing, and this is the one I'd want you to hear. If your compliance process is genuinely manual and email-based, automating it will make it faster. But if the actual constraint is that you don't have enough electrical contractors, then a faster process just makes people wait more efficiently.
[05:47] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): [pause] That's a very good point and it's one I've made internally.
[05:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What's the answer?
[05:55] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): I think it's both. I think there's a genuine contractor capacity issue and I also think we lose days to nobody chasing. But I couldn't tell you the split, which is —
[06:09] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which is the same problem.
[06:11] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): Which is exactly the same problem, yes. I can't tell you the split because I don't have the data, and I don't have the data because nothing's instrumented.
[06:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then can I suggest something that isn't a sale?
[06:26] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): Go on.
[06:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The first phase of something like this shouldn't be automating the voids process. It should be instrumenting it. Just recording state transitions — property became void, inspection booked, inspection done, works raised, works complete, compliance requested, certificate received, re-let. Timestamps only. No automation, no changing anyone's job.
[06:55] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): And then look at the data.
[06:58] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Run it for eight weeks and look at where the time actually goes. Then automate the two stages that turn out to matter, rather than the eight stages people complain about.
[07:11] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): That would be considerably cheaper.
[07:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's considerably cheaper and it's much easier to get through a procurement process, and if it turns out the answer is "you need more electricians", you've spent very little to find that out.
[07:28] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): You'd be arguing yourself down to a smaller deal.
[07:32] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd be arguing myself into a deal that survives. The ones that go wrong are the ones where we automate the wrong thing at scale.
[07:42] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): [pause] Alright. What do you want from me?
[07:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Half an hour, in the next couple of weeks, with you and whoever owns the housing management system technically. I'd want to understand the systems and I'd want to ask about procurement properly. No demo.
[08:03] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): No demo?
[08:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): If we get to a demo and it turns out we can't be procured or can't reach your housing system, I've wasted an hour of your life and mine.
[08:15] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): That's sensible. Our technical person is Priya Menon — she's our applications manager.
[08:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Would she come?
[08:25] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): If I ask her. She's sceptical of vendors, which I'd say is a feature.
[08:32] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's very much a feature. Ask her to bring the awkward questions.
[08:38] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): She won't need encouragement.
[08:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Good. Anything I should send beforehand?
[08:46] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): Two things. What you'd need from our housing management system technically — Priya will want to know that before the call, not during it. And anything you've got on other housing associations or public sector bodies.
[09:02] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll be honest — I don't have a housing association reference. We have public sector customers but not in your sector.
[09:12] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): [pause] That's a problem for procurement rather than for me.
[09:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd assumed so. I'd rather say it now.
[09:21] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): Say it to Priya as well. She'll ask.
[09:25] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I will. What about frameworks — can you tell me which ones you use so I can check whether we're on them?
[09:33] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): I'll send you a list. There are three we use routinely.
[09:38] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then I'll check before we meet, and if we're not on any of them I'll tell you and we can decide whether it's worth continuing.
[09:47] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): You keep offering to end this.
[09:50] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather have five real conversations than twenty polite ones.
[09:55] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): [laughs] Alright. Send me the technical requirements, I'll send you the frameworks, and I'll get Priya. Week of the sixth?
[10:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Week of the sixth. Thank you, Ade. That was a much better cold call than I expected.
[10:12] Ade Balogun (Head of Business Change, Beacon Housing Trust): It was a much better cold call than I expected too. Bye.

=== CALL-020 (call kind: cold_call)
CALL ID: CALL-020
DATE: 2026-09-30
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Kestrel Robotics
INDUSTRY: Industrial robotics
COMPANY SIZE: 150 employees
STAGE: Cold call
DURATION: 8 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Leo Grant, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Rafael Santos, COO, Kestrel Robotics
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Rafael.
[00:02] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Rafael, hi. Leo Grant, OrbitFlow. Cold call — I'll be quick and you can hang up.
[00:09] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] OrbitFlow. That's funny.
[00:13] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is it?
[00:15] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): We're three weeks into evaluating Tray.io. Your name came up on a list and got crossed off.
[00:23] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Crossed off by whom?
[00:25] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Me. About a month ago.
[00:28] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask why? Genuinely — I'm not going to argue, I just want to know.
[00:34] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Your website. It's very enterprise. Governance, compliance, workspace separation. We're a hundred and fifty people building robots. I looked at it and thought, that's not for us.
[00:49] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [pause] That's a fair read of our website.
[00:53] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You're agreeing?
[00:55] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Our marketing is aimed at companies with a governance function. You don't have one, so it isn't aimed at you.
[01:04] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): So why are you calling?
[01:06] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Because our marketing being aimed at somebody else doesn't mean the product is wrong for you. But I'd want to establish that in about four minutes rather than argue with your conclusion.
[01:19] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Go on then. Four minutes.
[01:22] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What are you trying to do with Tray?
[01:25] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Order-to-deployment. A customer orders a robot cell, and then there's engineering config, procurement of the long-lead parts, build scheduling, factory acceptance testing, shipping, and site commissioning. Seven stages, five systems, and about four months elapsed.
[01:47] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And what goes wrong?
[01:49] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Nothing goes wrong exactly. Things just take longer than they should because stage four doesn't know stage three finished until someone mentions it in a meeting.
[02:01] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How much of the four months is waiting?
[02:04] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] I don't know. That's part of why we're doing this.
[02:10] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Okay. How's the Tray evaluation going?
[02:14] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Well. Genuinely well. Their team's been good.
[02:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then I'd say two things. First, I'm not going to tell you Tray is bad. It isn't. We lose to them and we beat them and it usually comes down to fit rather than quality.
[02:32] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): What's the second?
[02:34] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Three weeks in, with a decision coming, I'd be the third horse in a two-horse race, and that's usually a waste of everyone's time.
[02:44] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You're talking yourself out of it again.
[02:47] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'm being realistic about it. Unless there's something in your evaluation that isn't going well, in which case I'd want to know what.
[02:57] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] There is one thing.
[03:00] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[03:02] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Our ERP. It's a mid-market system, quite niche in manufacturing. Tray don't have a connector and we're looking at building against its API, which our one back-end developer estimates at three weeks.
[03:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Do you believe the estimate?
[03:21] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [laughs] No.
[03:23] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Nobody ever does.
[03:25] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): It'll be six.
[03:27] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd want to be honest — there's a good chance we don't have a connector either. What's the system?
[03:34] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): I'd rather not say on a cold call, if that's alright.
[03:39] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Completely fine. Then let me answer it generally. If it's a mid-market manufacturing ERP, we probably don't have a native connector, and you'd be building against the API with our generic REST action. Which is the same three weeks. Or six.
[03:57] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): So no advantage.
[04:00] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No advantage on that specific point, no. There might be one on what happens afterwards — who maintains it, whether it's reusable across the seven stages — but that's a subtler argument and I'm not going to pretend it's decisive.
[04:17] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You keep doing this.
[04:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Doing what?
[04:21] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Conceding things.
[04:23] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather concede the things that are true and be believed on the things that aren't.
[04:29] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] Alright. What's the argument you would make?
[04:35] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Honestly, only one, and it's small. You said your one back-end developer would build the ERP integration. What happens when he's busy and someone in operations wants to change which stage triggers a notification?
[04:52] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): It waits.
[04:54] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): For how long?
[04:56] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] Depends. Weeks.
[04:59] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then the question for your evaluation — for either vendor — is whether the people who own the process can change the process without him. That's testable in a week and most evaluations don't test it.
[05:15] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): How would you test it?
[05:17] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Have someone in operations, not your developer, build one real workflow. Not with the developer sitting next to them. And see what happens.
[05:29] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] That's a good test.
[05:33] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the test that predicts whether you're happy in two years. Run it against Tray — I mean that, run it against Tray, you're three weeks in and it costs you nothing.
[05:46] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): And if they pass?
[05:48] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then buy Tray. You'll have made a good decision for a good reason.
[05:54] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [laughs] You are the strangest salesperson I've spoken to this year.
[05:59] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll take that.
[06:01] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Look — I'm not going to restart the evaluation. We've got a decision date and I'm not moving it.
[06:09] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I wouldn't ask you to.
[06:11] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): But I'll do this. Send me something short — not a deck — on how you'd approach the seven-stage thing, and specifically on the operations-can-change-it question. If we go with Tray and it doesn't work out, I'll know who to call.
[06:29] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather have that than a demo you sit through politely.
[06:34] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): When's the decision?
[06:36] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Mid-October. Fourteenth, I think, or thereabouts.
[06:42] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Would it be worth a thirty-minute call before mid-October? Not a pitch. I'd walk through how I'd structure the seven stages and you can use the thinking whichever vendor you pick.
[06:56] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You'd do that knowing we'll probably go with Tray?
[07:01] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You're a hundred and fifty people building robots. You'll be four hundred people in three years and you'll be buying something else. I'd rather be the person who was useful.
[07:14] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] That's a long game.
[07:17] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the only game in a market this small.
[07:21] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Alright. Send the note. If it's good I'll do the thirty minutes.
[07:27] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask one thing before you go?
[07:30] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Go on.
[07:32] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The four months. Have you got a number for what a month costs you?
[07:37] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): A month of delay on a cell? Roughly, we recognise revenue on commissioning, so — a month is a month of revenue on a two hundred thousand pound order.
[07:50] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And how many orders in flight?
[07:53] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Eleven at the moment.
[07:55] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then if instrumenting the seven stages tells you where two weeks are going, that's a much bigger number than either vendor's licence.
[08:05] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] That's the slide I need for my board, isn't it.
[08:10] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the slide you need regardless of who you buy from.
[08:14] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [laughs] Send the note, Leo.
[08:17] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I will. Thanks Rafael.
[08:20] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Bye.

answer.summary: Yes. The clearest inconsistencies are about whether SSO is on all plans or only Enterprise, whether monthly billing is available for Growth or Growth is annual-only, and whether native connectors cover customer systems or the stack is a mix of native and API-based integrations. There is also a no-code contradiction: one rep said every workflow is completely no-code, while others said not every workflow is no-code and some parts use JavaScript or expressions.

claims.statement: One OrbitFlow rep said SSO is included on all plans, but other reps said SAML SSO is Enterprise-only.
