context.text:
=== CALL-002 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-002
DATE: 2026-06-05
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: BrightPath Health
INDUSTRY: Digital health
COMPANY SIZE: 1,100 employees
STAGE: Technical discovery
DURATION: 34 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Jon Bell, Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow
- Priya Shah, Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health
- Elliot Greene, Security Architect, BrightPath Health
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Morning both. Priya, Elliot — thanks for the time.
[00:05] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Morning. Quick logistics thing before we start. Elliot has a hard stop at forty past. So can we do security first and everything else after he drops?
[00:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Absolutely, and honestly that's the right order anyway. If security's a no, the rest is theatre.
[00:25] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): I appreciate you saying that. Most vendors want to do the demo first and then act surprised.
[00:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I've been on the wrong end of that. Okay — Elliot, you drive. What's on your list?
[00:41] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Right. The list is: we need to resolve the BAA question, review your subprocessors, SSO and SCIM, understand retention, and confirm how US data is handled.
[00:57] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which of those is the gate?
[01:01] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): The BAA is the gate. If you can't offer one, we cannot use OrbitFlow for any workflow that may involve protected health information. That's not me being difficult, that's — that's just where we are.
[01:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Understood, and I want to be careful here because this is exactly the thing people fudge on sales calls. I'm not going to give you a yes on this call. What I will do is get you a written answer from our legal and compliance side within — Jon, what's realistic, a week?
[01:41] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): A week is realistic for a written position, yes.
[01:46] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): A written position is fine. A verbal "we're working on it" is not.
[01:52] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Agreed.
[01:55] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Okay. Baseline certifications?
[01:59] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): SOC 2 Type II is the baseline. SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning, both on Enterprise. Encryption in transit and at rest. Audit logs covering administrative and workflow events. Retention configurable within supported ranges. EU data residency available on Enterprise.
[02:22] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): EU. We're a US operation with a UK subsidiary. What's the default region?
[02:30] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Default depends on where the workspace is provisioned. I'd rather confirm the specifics in writing than guess at your architecture on a call.
[02:41] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Good. That's the right answer.
[02:45] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Elliot's tolerance for confident guessing is quite low.
[02:50] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): [crosstalk] It's zero. It's zero, Priya.
[02:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Noted.
[02:57] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Subprocessors. Do you publish a list, and do you notify on change?
[03:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): We publish the list and there's a notification mechanism for changes. The exact notice period is contractual, so — again, that's a document question not a call question.
[03:18] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Fine. Retention. Can I set it, and can I set it differently per workspace?
[03:26] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Configurable within supported ranges. Per-workspace granularity I'd want to check against your specific requirement, because there are limits.
[03:37] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): What's the floor?
[03:40] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I don't want to quote you a number I'd have to walk back. I'll put it in the pack.
[03:47] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Okay.
[03:50] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Can I add one? Environment separation. We'd want granular separation between sandbox and production — not just a flag, actual separation.
[04:03] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Workspace separation is supported, and Enterprise has stronger governance around who can publish where. What I'd want to understand is whether you mean separate data planes or separate logical workspaces, because those are very different asks.
[04:22] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Logical is probably enough. Elliot?
[04:26] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Logical is probably enough if the access controls are real and the audit trail crosses both.
[04:34] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's supportable.
[04:37] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Now the one I actually care about. What happens to data sent to an LLM provider?
[04:45] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Honest answer, it depends on configuration and provider, so I don't want to over-generalise. We use enterprise API arrangements where those exist, and providers are documented as subprocessors. For customers with stricter policies there are two options — disable AI entirely, or scope the initial phase to deterministic workflow steps and let security review model usage on a separate track.
[05:14] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): The second one. That separation would help a lot, actually. AI is interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation use case over.
[05:26] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's a bigger concession than you usually make.
[05:30] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): I'm aware.
[05:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Just so I capture it correctly — AI off for phase one, reviewed separately, not ruled out permanently?
[05:42] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Correct.
[05:45] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'll add — AI steps here are explicit, inspectable workflow steps. They're not ambient. Admins restrict which models are allowed, Enterprise can disable the features entirely, and we log the model configuration used on each run. We also don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
[06:09] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): That last sentence. Is it in the contract or is it on a marketing page?
[06:15] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It needs to be in the contract for you to rely on it, and I'd expect you to insist on that.
[06:22] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): I will insist on that.
[06:25] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Write it down, Elliot.
[06:27] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): It's written down.
[06:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What else can we send? SOC 2 report, subprocessor list, DPA, architecture diagram, retention documentation — is that the pack?
[06:42] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Add pen test summary. And yes. And we'll send you our questionnaire, which is long, and I apologise in advance.
[06:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): They're all long. We'll complete it.
[06:58] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): One more. Who at your end can see our run data?
[07:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Role-based access, workspace separation, and secrets are never displayed in run logs. Internally, support access is controlled and logged. If you need field-level masking for specific payloads, that's a design conversation rather than a checkbox.
[07:24] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): We will need that conversation. We have workflows where an admin should know a step failed without seeing the record contents.
[07:35] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yeah, that's a very common pattern in your sector. It's designable, I just don't want to say "yes, masking, done" when the real answer is "yes, with design".
[07:48] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Understood. Right, that's most of my list. I've got twenty-five minutes before I have to go. Priya, do you want to do current state so I can hear it?
[08:00] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Yes, let's.
[08:03] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please. What's actually broken today?
[08:08] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Two things, and they're linked. First, business teams request automations from a small systems group — my group — and there's a growing backlog. Second, compliance review slows down any workflow that touches patient-adjacent data, which is most of them.
[08:29] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How long's the backlog?
[08:32] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Currently? [pause] I'd say eleven weeks for anything non-trivial. It was six in January.
[08:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So it's getting worse.
[08:44] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): It's getting worse. And what happens when the backlog gets long is people route around us. Someone builds something in Power Automate, it works, they leave, and then it's nobody's.
[08:59] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Which is my problem, eventually.
[09:03] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Which becomes Elliot's problem, eventually, yes.
[09:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is it that the steps are manual, or —
[09:11] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): No, that's the thing. It's not that every step is manual, we have automation in places. The problem is the gaps between the automated pieces. Something fires, then there's a four-day hole where a human is supposed to notice, and sometimes they don't.
[09:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Do you have telemetry on that or is it anecdotal?
[09:36] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Mix. Outcome metrics exist. Operational telemetry is weak. We can usually tell you something was late after the fact. We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed, or whether the same failure happened fifteen times last month.
[09:57] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Can I correct something, actually, before we go further.
[10:02] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Go on.
[10:04] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): I said earlier — and I've said it in other meetings — that patient information never goes into HubSpot. Policy says it shouldn't. In practice we do occasionally find patient names in free-text fields. Which is exactly why I'm strict about the boundary. I don't want you designing against the policy version of our data.
[10:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's genuinely useful and it's not a small admission.
[10:36] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): It's not an admission, it's a control gap I'm managing. But yes.
[10:42] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): [laughs] Sorry.
[10:45] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): The process people describe and the process people run are not the same thing. That's true everywhere.
[10:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It is. Okay, let me play the stack back. HubSpot, Microsoft Teams, Azure, Databricks, Jira Service Management.
[11:05] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's it. Plus a lot of SharePoint that nobody admits to.
[11:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which is the system of record for the process?
[11:15] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Depends on the object. Customer and commercial data has a clear home. Tasks and tickets have a different home. And then a very large amount of actual context lives in chat, which — that's precisely why a workflow layer is interesting to us.
[11:36] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And you've got Power Automate today.
[11:40] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): We do. It's already covered by our Microsoft agreement, which matters a lot to procurement.
[11:48] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So what's the problem with it?
[11:51] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Complex flows are difficult to monitor. And ownership becomes unclear when the creator changes role, which happens constantly. So I want to be clear — I'm not sitting here saying we have no automation. The question is whether a different layer gives us better maintainability and operational control.
[12:15] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the right question, and we won't try to replace everything. Plenty of customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep integration and use us for business-owned workflows — the ones with human decisions, exceptions, cross-functional handoffs.
[12:35] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's closer to how we'd think about it. I'd be nervous if the proposal was migrate everything off Microsoft.
[12:44] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It isn't, and frankly that proposal would lose to your licensing agreement anyway.
[12:51] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): It would.
[12:54] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Let me try a phase-one candidate on you. Route implementation requests from HubSpot into Jira, enrich them with account data, notify Teams, track exceptions — and do all of that without copying sensitive notes into three more systems.
[13:14] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That last clause is the important one. Yes, that's a good candidate.
[13:20] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): The "without copying" part is not a nice-to-have.
[13:25] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Understood. And that's a real design constraint — you'd want to pass references rather than payloads wherever possible, and only pull the sensitive field at the point of use, if at all.
[13:39] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Yes. Exactly that.
[13:43] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): One caveat on the workflow, though. The happy path is not the hard part.
[13:50] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[13:52] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): I want to see what happens when data's missing, when an API times out, when an approver does nothing for two days, when the account changes state after the workflow's already started.
[14:07] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's the right level to test at. Workflows are event-driven but each run holds state. Branch on data, pause for approvals, retry external actions, set timeout rules, push an exception into a queue rather than failing silently.
[14:26] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Can the queue be owned by a team rather than a named individual? People change roles constantly here and individual ownership is one of the main reasons our current automations rot.
[14:41] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes. Route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. Run history persists so an admin can see inputs, which steps ran, and where it stopped.
[14:57] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Good. [pause] That's — sorry, that's my calendar. I've got about ten minutes.
[15:06] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Anything else you need before you go?
[15:10] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): One thing. Can we export audit logs to our own SIEM, or do they live in your console?
[15:19] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Run events and metrics via APIs and webhooks, and audit export on Enterprise. Several customers forward failures into their incident tooling.
[15:31] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): That's what I wanted to hear. If it only lives in your console it's not an audit trail, it's a screenshot.
[15:40] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): [laughs] I'm going to steal that.
[15:44] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Please do. Right, last one from me. Priya mentioned a second use case earlier and I want to flag my position on it.
[15:54] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Go ahead.
[15:56] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): The idea is to give operations teams a governed way to build simple workflows without receiving broad access to production systems. I'm supportive of that in principle. In practice it lives or dies on whether the permission model is genuinely least-privilege or just a UI that hides things.
[16:20] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a fair challenge and I'd want to demo the permission model specifically rather than hand-wave it.
[16:29] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Then let's do that in the next session. Right — I have to go. Priya, you've got my notes. Thanks both.
[16:39] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thanks Elliot, appreciate the directness.
[16:43] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): [inaudible] — thanks.
[16:47] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Okay. He's off. He's actually much friendlier than that.
[16:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): He was completely reasonable. I'd rather have that than someone who says yes to everything and then blocks it in week nine.
[17:03] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Mm. That has happened.
[17:07] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Can I tell a slightly relevant story?
[17:10] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Sure.
[17:12] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Before this I was on-call for a data platform at a company I won't name. And we had an integration that had been running fine for eleven months, and then one Tuesday at three in the morning it started silently dropping about four percent of records. Not failing — dropping.
[17:34] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Oh no.
[17:36] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Took us nine days to find. And the reason it took nine days is the exact thing you described — we could see that something was wrong downstream, we could not see which step, when, or how often. That's genuinely why I care about run history more than I care about the connector catalogue.
[17:58] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Nine days.
[18:00] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Nine days. I still think about it.
[18:04] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): We had something similar with a HubSpot sync. Not nine days. Four. But similar.
[18:12] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Shall we do the build, Jon?
[18:15] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yeah. Sharing now. [pause] Priya, can you see the builder?
[18:22] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Yes.
[18:24] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): So — triggers and actions on the left, the flow in the middle, config for the selected step on the right. A workflow can start from a SaaS event, a schedule, a webhook, a database query, or another workflow.
[18:41] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'll start this one from a record-change event, validate a few required fields, enrich from a second system, then branch. And the thing I want to emphasise, particularly for you given the backlog problem — we push people hard towards small reusable components. If your systems group builds ten good subflows, account lookup, approval, notification, incident creation, then the marginal cost of the eleventh business request drops a lot.
[19:14] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's — okay, that's actually the interesting bit for me. That's the backlog answer, potentially.
[19:23] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It's the one that compounds, yes.
[19:27] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): How technical is it really? Because every vendor says no-code until you hit the one thing the connector doesn't do.
[19:37] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Fair, and I won't pretend. Mapping and branching are visual. Transformations use expressions. On Enterprise you can package reusable JavaScript steps. There's a generic REST action and webhooks. We don't claim every workflow is no-code. The goal is that the workflow stays understandable even when an engineer supplied one custom component.
[20:04] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's a better answer than pretending my team will never touch code. I want to reduce dependency, not eliminate engineers.
[20:14] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Right, and in your case I'd argue the goal is to move your systems group up the stack — they build the components, the business assembles them.
[20:26] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's the model I've been trying to sell internally for two years.
[20:32] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's make that explicit in the pilot criteria rather than leaving it implied.
[20:38] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Yes. Please.

[20:59] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Can I see a failed one?
[21:02] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yeah. [pause] So this one timed out on the third step, retried twice, then routed to the exception queue. And you can see the payload it was carrying at the point of failure — which, for you, is precisely the thing you'd want masked.
[21:22] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Yes. Elliot would have opinions about that screen.
[21:27] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Elliot should have opinions about that screen.
[21:31] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): What about schema changes? We've had integrations break because someone renamed a field and nothing said anything.
[21:40] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): We cache metadata but refresh it, and mapping errors surface on the run. For high-impact flows I'd recommend explicit validation at the start rather than assuming every source field is populated. You can also alert when error rates cross a threshold.
[22:00] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): I'd want that in the evaluation. A demo with clean data proves nothing.
[22:07] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then give us messy data. Genuinely.
[22:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Integrations — you'd said HubSpot, Teams, Jira and Azure AD are the important ones, and Databricks would be via API initially?
[22:23] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's right. Databricks is not phase one. I put it on the list so you'd tell me if it was impossible.
[22:32] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It's not impossible. It's API work.
[22:36] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which one's the deal-breaker if it doesn't work well?
[22:41] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): The system of record. If that connector's unreliable none of the rest matters. After that, the collaboration and data systems, because that's where context goes missing.
[22:55] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): For your stack it's a mix of native connectors and API-based options. In a pilot I'd want to validate each required operation rather than pointing at a logo on our integrations page.
[23:10] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Good, because I have been burned by the logo page.
[23:15] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Everyone has. [pause] Sorry, is that — is that an alarm at your end?
[23:22] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): It's a fire alarm test. It's Friday. They do it every Friday at half eleven and every Friday I forget.
[23:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Do you need to —
[23:33] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): No, no, it's a test, it stops in about — [pause] there. Gone. Sorry.
[23:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No problem.
[23:44] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Where were we.
[23:46] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Commercials, if you're happy to.
[23:50] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Go on then.

[24:15] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Honestly? I'm not ready to react to that.
[24:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's fine.

[24:38] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's completely logical and I'm not going to push. What I'd ask is that when we do get to it, you let me build the model around your actual user population rather than a headline number.
[24:53] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): What counts as a user? Because we'd have a small number of builders and a lot of people who only approve something or get a notification.
[25:04] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Builders and full workspace users are the licensed ones. Approval-only or notification-only can be structured differently depending on package. I'm deliberately not quoting you a figure today because without the user model any figure I give is misleading.
[25:23] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Please make that explicit in the proposal when it comes. I don't want to discover in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
[25:35] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It'll be itemised. Assumed builders, viewer and approver population, expected workflow volume, one-time services separately.
[25:46] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Thank you.
[25:49] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How would you make the ROI case internally? Headcount, cycle time, errors, engineering maintenance?
[25:58] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Not headcount. I wouldn't sell it that way and it also isn't true. The stronger case is consistency and speed. We've got expensive people doing coordination work because the systems don't carry enough process context. And there's the backlog cost, which is harder to quantify but it's real — eleven weeks of waiting has a number attached to it somewhere.
[26:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): For a pilot we can baseline one or two things before automating. Elapsed time, manual touches, exception rate, or systems-group hours spent on requests.
[26:40] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): The last one. That's the one my director cares about.
[26:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then that's the baseline.
[26:48] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): I'd also measure adoption. A technically correct workflow that everyone routes around is a failed implementation. That's literally what happened with our last internal tool.
[27:02] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Who owns this day to day if it goes ahead?
[27:07] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): I'm the sponsor — business systems. Security can veto, as you've seen. Privacy counsel reviews the DPA and the BAA. Procurement handles final terms.
[27:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Four gates.
[27:24] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Four gates. Welcome to healthcare.
[27:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And operationally?
[27:31] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): A small central group owning standards, business teams contributing requirements. With naming conventions, change control on the important ones, and a rule that someone other than the creator can understand each production flow.
[27:48] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That matches what we recommend. A few centrally owned templates, defined publishing rights, dev separated from prod.
[27:58] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Do you have version history? If someone changes a condition on a Friday and it breaks, can we see what changed?

[28:23] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Yes. That's closer to a real deployment.
[28:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Timing. What are we working towards?
[28:32] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): No production launch before Q4. That's firm. But we could run a non-sensitive proof of concept in August — synthetic data, or clearly non-PHI.
[28:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What has to be true to move from evaluation to a decision?
[28:53] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): One representative workflow working with real enough data. The security gates understood, and by understood I mean answered. A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises. And the people who'd operate it believing they can own it.
[29:12] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And the honest alternative?
[29:15] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Power Automate. Or just improving what we already have. Those are the real competitors, not another workflow vendor.
[29:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's define the pilot against the status quo and against Power Automate. And I'll say the same thing I said to Elliot — a valid outcome is "don't buy OrbitFlow" if the existing approach meets the criteria more cheaply.
[29:44] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): I'll hold you to that.
[29:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please do.
[29:50] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): So — where does that leave us. My read is I would still consider a limited pilot with synthetic or clearly non-PHI data. But I want to be explicit about something: a successful pilot would not automatically mean we can deploy broadly. Those are two different decisions and they have different approvers.
[30:15] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's understood and I'd rather you said it now.
[30:20] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Good.
[30:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Concrete next steps then. We send the security pack — SOC 2, subprocessors, DPA, architecture diagram, retention docs, pen test summary. Separately, and this is the one that matters, a written position on the BAA within a week. You send us the representative workflow and some sample data, ideally messy. And we jointly write three to five pilot success criteria.
[30:53] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): And a session on the permission model for Elliot.
[30:58] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And a session on the permission model for Elliot. Jon, can you own that?
[31:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yeah. I'd want an hour and I'd want Elliot to bring his worst-case scenario rather than me showing him a clean one.
[31:14] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): He will have one ready. He always has one ready.
[31:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Let me summarise. You don't need automation for its own sake. The opportunity is a systems group that builds components rather than fulfilling tickets, and a small number of cross-system processes that are observable and less dependent on individuals. The blocker is regulatory, not technical, and until it's answered nothing else moves.
[31:47] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's an accurate summary.
[31:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): One more thing — can you write down the assumptions we made today? Some of what you told me was approximate and I don't want it hardening into a requirement by accident.
[32:04] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): You want me to do that?
[32:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No, sorry — I'll do that. I'll send a recap with open questions separated from confirmed requirements.
[32:16] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Ah. Yes. That would be useful, actually, because half of what I said about the backlog was from memory.
[32:25] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then it goes in the open questions column.
[32:29] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Great. Thanks both. And apologies again for the alarm.
[32:35] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Genuinely the least disruptive thing that's happened to me this week.
[32:41] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): [laughs] Bye.
[32:44] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thanks Priya.

question: Is Ember Financial likely to choose OrbitFlow over Tray.io?
correct_reason: The main point is right: the evidence is mixed and there's no decision yet, and most factors are covered. One required core is missing: the known gap that OrbitFlow can't enforce AI outputs staying leaf nodes.

verdicts.reason: The answer says there's no final decision and Ember is still evaluating, and it weighs evidence on both sides.
It quotes Noah saying 'I want to move' and asking for sandbox access and a six-week pilot proposal. It doesn't mention Hannah saying her gates were addressed.
It covers Tray's six-week head start and the cheaper 'keep the scripts' option. It doesn't say Tray's connector breadth is genuinely good.
It names debugging and programmatic audit export as the deciding factors, and says connector breadth is a tie.
It never mentions that the platform can't enforce AI outputs staying leaf nodes.

result.question: Is Ember Financial likely to choose OrbitFlow over Tray.io?

context.text:
=== CALL-005 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-005
DATE: 2026-07-02
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Ember Financial
INDUSTRY: Fintech
COMPANY SIZE: 900 employees
STAGE: Evaluation
DURATION: 31 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Leo Grant, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Nina Patel, Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow
- Noah Williams, VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial
- Hannah Cole, Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Morning Noah, morning Hannah. Nina's joining in a couple of minutes, she's coming off another call.
[00:07] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): No problem. Shall I set the frame?
[00:11] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please.
[00:13] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): So you should know we're running this as a bake-off. You and Tray.io. We've had a Tray proof of concept running for about six weeks. This isn't a discovery call for us, we know what we want. This is us testing whether you can do it.
[00:31] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the most useful opening I've had this month. Can I ask what the Tray PoC has shown you?
[00:39] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Connector breadth is genuinely good. No complaints there.
[00:44] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): The engineers hate debugging it.
[00:47] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Hannah's being blunt but she's not wrong. Large visual workflows are hard for our people to reason about. When something goes wrong at step forty of a sixty-step flow, the debugging experience is — it's not good.
[01:04] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a fair criticism of the category, honestly, not just of them. Big visual workflows are hard to debug everywhere. What we'd argue is composition — small subflows rather than one enormous canvas — but I'd rather Nina show you that than me claim it.
[01:25] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): We'll test it either way.
[01:28] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You should.
[01:30] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): The other thing you should know is who has to be convinced. I'm the executive sponsor and I'm broadly positive. Hannah and platform engineering score technical fit. Then security, legal, procurement, and the COO approve. So there are a lot of ways for this to die and only one way for it to happen.
[01:53] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which of those is most likely to kill it?
[01:57] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Me.
[01:58] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): [laughs] Hannah.
[02:00] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): I'm not joking. The main gates are model-risk and auditability. If you can't satisfy those, connector breadth will not save the project. It doesn't matter how many logos are on the integrations page.
[02:16] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's do those two first and I'll let Nina take most of it. Nina, are you —
[02:23] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'm here. Sorry. Sorry, I was on mute. I'm here.
[02:28] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Perfect timing. Hannah's just said model risk and auditability are the gates and everything else is decoration.
[02:36] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Right. Okay. Hannah, can you define what you mean by model risk in your context? Because in financial services that phrase means something specific and I don't want to answer a different question.
[02:51] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): [pause] Good. Most vendors just start talking.
[02:56] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I used to work in payments. I've been on your side of this call.
[03:02] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Then you'll know. We have a model risk management framework. Anything that produces an output which influences a decision has to be documented, validated, monitored, and periodically reviewed. If your product puts a language model in a decision path, that model is in scope, and getting something into scope is a nine-month process here.
[03:28] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): So the question isn't "is your AI good", it's "does using it drag us into model governance."
[03:36] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Exactly that.

answer.summary: Ember Financial is likely to keep OrbitFlow in serious contention, but the call does not show a committed win over Tray.io yet. The strongest signal is Noah’s request to “compare it against Tray properly” and move to a six-week pilot, while Hannah says OrbitFlow would win if its debugging and audit export are better; she also corrects the framing to say Tray has a six-week head start, which makes OrbitFlow the underdog. This is an inference from the calls, not a commitment to buy.

question: Are Inkwell Learning's account-health scores reliable enough to drive the at-risk workflow?

penalties_hit.reason: The answer gives a flat, high-confidence 'No' and does not report the untested signal. It is not a hedged 'probably not' covering both points, and it presents an impression as hard evidence.

correct_reason: The answer flatly concludes, with high confidence, that the scores are unreliable. It relies on Darren's impression as if it were a measurement and leaves out the untested signal, the backtest plan and the agreed design. That makes the penalty hit on the main point, even though the disagreement itself is reported.

verdicts.reason: The answer describes the disagreement between Olivia ('directionally useful') and Darren ('noise with a trend in them').
The answer treats Darren's 'fewer than half' claim as established evidence and never says it was only his impression rather than a measurement.
The agreed design, where machine signals (Snowflake, Zendesk) carry the flag and Salesforce fields are shown only as context, is not mentioned.
The answer does not say the signal is untested or that Darren will backtest past escalations before any purchase.

context.text:
=== CALL-009 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-009
DATE: 2026-08-04
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Inkwell Learning
INDUSTRY: Education technology
COMPANY SIZE: 520 employees
STAGE: Solution evaluation
DURATION: 31 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Jon Bell, Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow
- Olivia Grant, SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning
- Darren Wu, Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Hi Olivia, hi Darren. Olivia, I know you've got a hard stop at half past so I'll keep us moving.
[00:08] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Thank you. I do, unfortunately.
[00:11] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I can stay on after if it's useful.
[00:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That'd be helpful, actually. Where I'd like to start is the use case, because we've had two rounds of email on it and I want to make sure we're solving the same problem.
[00:26] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Yes. So — support volume spikes around school-term launches. Enormously. And the problem isn't the volume itself, we can staff for volume. The problem is that we struggle to distinguish isolated tickets from account-level implementation risk until the escalation reaches an executive.
[00:49] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So by the time you know, it's already senior.
[00:53] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): By the time I know, a school district's chief of staff has emailed our CEO. That's the current detection mechanism and it is not a good one.
[01:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How often?
[01:07] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Four or five times a term. Which sounds small until you remember each one is a renewal at risk.
[01:16] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Can I complicate this before we go further?
[01:20] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Go ahead, he's going to anyway.
[01:23] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] I am. So — the proposal, as I understand it, is to combine Zendesk ticket patterns, Salesforce account status, and Snowflake product usage to flag accounts needing proactive intervention, and create structured follow-up tasks.
[01:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's how I've written it down, yes.
[01:44] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Right. And my concern is not whether that's technically possible. It obviously is. My concern is data quality. If Salesforce fields are stale, an elegant workflow will still make bad decisions. Beautifully, consistently, at scale.
[02:04] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a fair challenge and I'd rather have it now.
[02:09] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): There's a specific version of it, actually, and I want to challenge something Olivia said in the last session.
[02:16] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Here we go.
[02:18] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Olivia talks about account-health scores as though they're reliable. Leadership uses them, they're on the QBR deck, they're in the board pack. But fewer than half our CSMs update the underlying fields consistently. So I would not treat those scores as ground truth, and if we build a workflow that keys off them we've automated a guess.
[02:44] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's — I don't entirely disagree.
[02:49] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): You've disagreed before.
[02:52] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I've disagreed with the framing. I think the scores are directionally useful and you think they're noise.
[03:00] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I think they're noise with a trend in them, which is not the same as useful.
[03:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask a question that might be helpful here?
[03:11] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Please.
[03:13] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Of the three data sources — Zendesk tickets, Salesforce status, Snowflake usage — which one do you both actually trust?
[03:23] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [immediately] Snowflake.
[03:25] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [crosstalk] Snowflake, yes.
[03:27] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because it's machine-generated. Nobody has to remember to update it.
[03:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And Zendesk?
[03:35] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Reasonably good. Ticket volume and category are reliable. The sentiment tagging is not, because it's manual.
[03:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And Salesforce.
[03:47] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Salesforce is reliable for the commercial facts — contract dates, ARR, owner. It is unreliable for anything a human has to remember to type.
[04:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's actually a very clean answer and I think it's the design.
[04:06] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Say more.
[04:08] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Weight the signals by how they're produced. Machine-generated usage data and structured ticket data carry the flag. Human-maintained fields are context you show to the person, not inputs the logic depends on.
[04:26] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's — yes. That's the right architecture.
[04:32] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Would that actually have caught the escalations we've had?
[04:37] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's the question, isn't it.
[04:40] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can you test it? You've got history.
[04:44] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): How would we test it?
[04:47] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Take the escalations that reached you and run them backwards. For each one, look at what the usage data and ticket data looked like three weeks earlier. If the signal was there, you've got a case. If it wasn't, you've saved yourself a project.
[05:05] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): We could do that with SQL. We don't need a workflow platform to do that.
[05:11] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You absolutely don't, and you should do it before you buy anything from us.
[05:17] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] Alright. That's not the answer I expected.
[05:22] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): If the signal isn't in the data, we can't manufacture it. And I'd rather you found that out with a query than with a pilot.
[05:32] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Darren, could you do that?
[05:35] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I could do that in a day. Maybe two.
[05:39] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Then why haven't we?
[05:41] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because nobody's asked me to, and because I've been arguing about the health scores instead.
[05:48] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] Fair.
[05:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd suggest making it the first thing, honestly. It's the cheapest way to find out whether this project should exist.
[05:59] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I'm slightly surprised you're saying that.
[06:03] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): If it turns out the signal isn't there, you'd discover it in month three of a pilot and I'd have burned your goodwill and my quarter. I'd rather know in week one.
[06:16] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Alright. Darren, do it.
[06:19] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I'll do it.
[06:21] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask what you'd look for? Because the answer isn't binary.
[06:26] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Meaning?
[06:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Meaning it's rarely "the signal was there" or "it wasn't." It's usually "it was there for six of the twelve, and for four of those it was there so early it'd have been indistinguishable from noise."
[06:43] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's a good point. So I'd want the lead time as well as the presence.
[06:50] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And the false positive rate. How many accounts looked the same and turned out fine.
[06:57] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] Yes. That's the harder half.
[07:02] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Why harder?
[07:04] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because to measure false positives I need to know which accounts were fine, and "fine" isn't recorded anywhere. Absence of escalation isn't the same as fine.
[07:17] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): No, it isn't.
[07:20] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): For what it's worth, that's a problem you'd have with any approach, including buying Gainsight properly. It's not an OrbitFlow problem.
[07:31] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Speaking of which. You should know what we've got.
[07:35] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[07:37] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Customer success uses a limited Gainsight deployment. Limited meaning we bought it, we implemented about forty percent of it, and then the person who owned it left.
[07:51] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): And my team has built a set of Looker alerts. Which work, but they're alerts. They tell you something and then nothing happens.
[08:02] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So neither gives you the cross-system workflow.
[08:07] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Neither gives us the workflow. Gainsight has the customer success concepts but we haven't implemented them. Looker has the data but no ability to make anything happen. And nothing joins Zendesk to Snowflake to Salesforce in a way that produces an action.
[08:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is expanding Gainsight the real alternative?
[08:32] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): It's the alternative someone will propose, yes.
[08:36] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's the alternative I'd propose if the cost comparison favoured it.
[08:42] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's do that comparison honestly rather than pretending it isn't the competition.
[08:49] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I'd want that. A cost model comparing this with expanding Gainsight. Including the implementation effort on both sides, because the forty-percent thing wasn't a licensing failure, it was an implementation failure.
[09:06] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a genuinely useful distinction and I'll build the comparison that way.
[09:12] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): You'll build a comparison that includes your competitor fairly?
[09:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll build one that includes them accurately. Whether it's fair is for you to judge, and you should check my numbers.
[09:26] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] Alright.
[09:29] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Shall I show something? Because there's a shape here I want to check with Darren.
[09:35] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Go on.
[09:37] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Sharing. [pause] So this is a workflow that's roughly the pattern we're describing. It's scheduled rather than event-driven — it runs daily, queries the warehouse, joins against the CRM, and evaluates a set of conditions.
[09:56] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Where does the query live?
[10:00] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): In the workflow, in this case. But you can also point at a view you own in Snowflake, which for you is probably better.
[10:10] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Much better. I don't want business logic living in two places.
[10:16] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then the pattern is: you own the definition of "at risk" as a view in Snowflake, we consume it and act on it. The intelligence is yours, the orchestration is ours.
[10:30] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's the first time a vendor has said that to me.
[10:35] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It's the only version that survives contact with a BI team.
[10:40] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It really is.
[10:43] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): What does "act on it" mean concretely?
[10:47] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): In this flow — create a structured follow-up task with the account, the signal that triggered it, and links back to the underlying tickets and usage. Assign it to the account's CSM, or to a queue if the owner field is stale. Escalate if nothing happens in N days.
[11:09] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): The escalation. That's the bit I want.
[11:13] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And it's the bit that's usually missing. An alert with no escalation path is a notification, and notifications get ignored.
[11:23] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): They do. I've got a Slack channel full of them.
[11:28] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's my channel and I take that personally.
[11:32] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] It's not personal, it's just full.
[11:36] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Can the escalation go to a team rather than a named person? Because "assign to CSM" breaks the moment someone changes role.
[11:47] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): That happens constantly.
[11:50] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then route to a group, resolve dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. And run history persists so you can see the inputs, which steps ran, and where it stopped.
[12:04] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): What happens when the workflow makes a bad call? Flags something that's fine.
[12:11] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a good question and the honest answer is you need a feedback path or the thing degrades. If a CSM dismisses a flag, that dismissal should be recorded, and you should look at dismissal rates as a health metric for the workflow itself.
[12:29] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Does the platform do that or do we build it?
[12:33] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You build it. It's a field on the task and a report. I'm not going to tell you there's a built-in model-monitoring feature, because there isn't.
[12:44] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Thank you.
[12:46] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Why does everyone thank them for saying no?
[12:50] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because it's rare.
[12:52] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] We get that a lot.
[12:56] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): What about the second thing? The weekly narrative summary.
[13:01] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the AI use case. As I've got it written: produce a weekly narrative summary of emerging customer themes, with links back to supporting tickets and account records.
[13:14] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Yes. Because I currently get a spreadsheet and I don't read it.
[13:20] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I make that spreadsheet.
[13:22] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I know. I'm sorry.
[13:25] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's fine, I don't read it either.
[13:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Well, that's clarifying.
[13:32] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): The links back are the important part and I'm glad you specified them. The way we'd build it is that the source references are stored alongside the generated output, so whoever reads the summary can click through to the tickets that produced each claim.
[13:51] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Because otherwise it's just a plausible paragraph.
[13:56] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Otherwise it's a plausible paragraph, yes. And plausible paragraphs are exactly what these models are best at, which is the problem.
[14:06] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Can it say "I don't know"? If there isn't a theme this week, will it invent one?
[14:13] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It will if you let it. You can design against that — require a minimum number of supporting tickets before a theme is reported, and route thin cases to review rather than publishing them. What I wouldn't do is rely on the model's own confidence score as a guarantee. The better control is evidence plus workflow policy.
[14:38] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Meaning the workflow refuses, not the model.
[14:42] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Meaning the workflow refuses. Yes.
[14:46] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's a meaningful distinction and most people blur it.
[14:51] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Can we see the prompt?
[14:53] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes. AI steps are explicit, inspectable workflow steps — you can see the prompt, the model, the configuration. Administrators can restrict which models are allowed, and Enterprise customers can disable AI features entirely. We log the model configuration used on each run, and we don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
[15:19] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): That last one matters for us.
[15:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd assumed it would. Which brings us to security, and I'd like to hear your list.
[15:29] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Darren, you've got it.
[15:32] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): SSO, audit logs, retention controls, and a clear boundary around student-level data. That last one is the important one.
[15:43] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Tell me what "clear boundary" means in practice.
[15:47] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): FERPA. We handle data about students in US school districts. Student-level records are subject to specific protections and our position is that they should never leave our warehouse.
[16:03] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): So the workflow operates on account-level aggregates only.
[16:09] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Correct. Usage counts, engagement rates, ticket volumes at the account level. Never a student record, never a student identifier.
[16:20] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's very cleanly specifiable, and it's the sort of constraint that's much easier to enforce if you define it in the Snowflake view rather than in our workflow.
[16:33] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] Because then it's impossible rather than forbidden.
[16:38] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Because then it's impossible rather than forbidden. If the view we consume contains no student-level columns, no workflow can leak them regardless of who builds it.
[16:51] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's the design. That's exactly the design.
[16:56] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Is that a FERPA answer or an engineering answer?
[17:01] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's an engineering answer that makes the FERPA answer easy. Our counsel would much rather hear "the data never leaves" than "the vendor has controls."
[17:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd note that we should still complete your security review properly. Making the data question moot doesn't remove the vendor assessment.
[17:24] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): No, but it makes it a normal one rather than a special one.
[17:29] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): On the rest of your list — SOC 2 Type II baseline, SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise, encryption in transit and at rest, audit logs covering administrative and workflow events, retention configurable within supported ranges. Run events and metrics through APIs and webhooks, audit export on Enterprise.
[17:53] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's sufficient for us. We're not a bank.
[17:57] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): We are occasionally treated like one by district procurement.
[18:02] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): True. Some districts have their own questionnaire.
[18:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Would we need to complete those?
[18:10] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Possibly, for the larger ones. Not for a pilot.
[18:15] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Good to know it's coming, though.
[18:18] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I've got about ten minutes. Can we do money?
[18:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yes. Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement. Enterprise is custom priced and adds the advanced governance, the security capabilities, and higher usage.
[18:38] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I think the price is reasonable if it lets us consolidate several manual programmes.
[18:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which programmes?
[18:47] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): The spreadsheet Darren makes. The at-risk review meeting, which is ninety minutes a week of expensive people reading a list. And a chunk of what we're notionally paying Gainsight for.
[19:03] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Olivia, we're not going to switch off Gainsight.
[19:07] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I know we're not going to switch it off. I'm saying the spend is questionable.
[19:13] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): The spend is very questionable. But that's a separate fight.
[19:19] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): It's a related fight.
[19:22] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] It's a related fight.

[20:19] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Sixty-two.
[20:21] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Sixty-two.
[20:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then that split goes in the proposal explicitly with the assumptions next to it. I won't quote a figure today because without that split any figure I give would mislead you in one direction or the other.

[20:56] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Thank you.

[21:32] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Which is why finance is sceptical of customer success business cases generally.
[21:38] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is there a leading indicator you could commit to instead? Something measurable that isn't the renewal itself.
[21:47] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Such as?

[22:11] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's a better framing than the one we've been using.
[22:16] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): It is. Write that down.
[22:19] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I'm writing it down.
[22:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And I'd add — Inkwell wants to measure whether the system identifies at-risk accounts earlier than the current process. That's the actual success criterion and it's testable against history.
[22:37] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Which brings us back to Darren's backward-looking analysis.
[22:42] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Everything brings us back to that.
[22:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the load-bearing question.
[22:48] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Decision process, quickly, because I need to go. I sponsor it. [23:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Who can say no?
[23:13] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Darren can effectively say no. Security can say no. Finance can say not yet, which is the same thing in practice.
[23:24] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I wouldn't say no out of principle. I'd say no if the data doesn't support it.
[23:31] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I know. That's why you're on the call.

[23:54] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So late September is a real date.
[23:58] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): It's a real date. And term starts in early September, which means everyone in customer success is unavailable for the first two weeks.
[24:09] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Which means August is the month.
[24:12] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): August is the month, and it's the fourth today.
[24:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's not spend two weeks arranging things. What's the fastest useful next step?
[24:24] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Darren's analysis, obviously.
[24:27] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I can have that by the end of next week.
[24:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And if the signal is there?
[24:34] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Then I want to pilot it. [25:30] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Snowflake, yes — we have history, I can reconstruct point-in-time. Zendesk, mostly. Salesforce, no. Salesforce fields get overwritten, there's no history on most of them.
[25:47] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Which is convenient, in a way, because you've already said the Salesforce human-maintained fields shouldn't carry the flag.
[25:56] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] That's true. The data limitation and the design decision agree with each other.
[26:04] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): That's the most encouraging thing I've heard today.
[26:08] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's coincidence.

[26:13] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Right, I have to go. Maya, what do you owe us?

The cost model comparing us with expanding Gainsight, including implementation effort on both sides. And a written recap separating what you confirmed today from what you estimated.
[26:41] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): What did we estimate?
[26:43] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Four or five escalations a term. Fewer than half of CSMs updating fields consistently. Ninety minutes a week on the review meeting. Sixty-two CSMs was firm, the rest were approximate.
[26:59] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): The "fewer than half" is an impression, not a measurement.
[27:04] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then it goes in the estimates column, and it's probably worth measuring since it affects the design.
[27:12] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's worth measuring regardless.
[27:15] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Add it to your list.
[27:18] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): My list is getting long.
[27:20] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] Thanks both. Genuinely useful. Darren, stay on if you've got questions.
[27:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thanks Olivia.
[27:30] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Bye.
[27:33] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Right. Two things I didn't want to raise in front of her.
[27:38] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[27:40] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): First — if we do this, the workflow logic has to be in version control somehow. Or at least reviewable. I'm not having business-critical logic that only exists in a web UI.
[27:55] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Version history and change metadata are there, so you can see what changed and when. Definitions can be exported through the API. Whether that satisfies you as version control depends on what you mean — it's not a git integration.
[28:12] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's not git.
[28:14] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It's not git. I'm not going to pretend it is.
[28:18] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Can I diff two versions?
[28:21] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You can see change metadata and version history in the product. A true side-by-side diff of two workflow definitions — I'd want to confirm what the export gives you rather than promise a diff experience.
[28:36] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Add it to the written list.
[28:39] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Adding it.
[28:41] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Second thing. What happens when I leave?
[28:45] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): [pause] Are you leaving?
[28:48] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): No. But the last person who owned Gainsight left and that's why we implemented forty percent of it. I want to know that if I get hit by a bus, someone else can pick this up.
[29:03] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's the right question and it's mostly not a product answer. The product parts are: workflows built as small readable subflows rather than one enormous canvas, version history so someone can see what changed, and run history so someone can see what actually happens. The rest is your operating model — naming conventions, a rule that someone other than the builder can understand each production flow, documentation as a deliverable rather than a hope.
[29:36] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): So the answer is "it depends on us."
[29:40] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Largely, yes. What I'd say is that this platform makes it possible. It doesn't make it happen.
[29:48] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's the honest answer.
[29:51] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): If I told you the tool solves organisational memory I'd be lying to you.
[29:57] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): People have.
[29:59] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'm sure.
[30:02] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Alright. I'll do the backward analysis and I'll be honest about what it shows. If the signal's not there I'll say so and we'll stop.
[30:13] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's all I'd want.
[30:16] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): And if it is there, I'll be more enthusiastic than I've been today.
[30:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You've been fine. Sceptical isn't unfriendly.
[30:26] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] My last three managers would disagree.
[30:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thanks Darren. Good luck with the query.
[30:35] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Thanks. Bye.
[30:37] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Bye.
