context.text:
=== CALL-007 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-007
DATE: 2026-07-16
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Greenline Energy Services
INDUSTRY: Renewable energy field services
COMPANY SIZE: 2,300 employees
STAGE: Discovery
DURATION: 27 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Jon Bell, Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow (joined at 09:12)
- Carlos Mendes, Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services
- Lucy Hart, Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Hi both. Quick heads up — Jon, our solutions engineer, is stuck on another call and will join around ten past. So it's me for the first bit, which means if you ask me something deeply technical I'll write it down rather than guess.
[00:16] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): That's fine. Can you hear me alright? I'm at a site, the line's not brilliant.
[00:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You're a bit windy but you're clear.
[00:25] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): [laughs] Story of my life.
[00:28] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): I'm at a desk, so if Carlos drops I can carry on.
[00:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Perfect. So — tell me what's actually happening today.
[00:38] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Right. So the core of it is field exceptions. An installation gets blocked — equipment hasn't turned up, or somebody doesn't have the right permission, or access to the site isn't arranged. And the thing is, that exception is visible. It's in the system.
[00:57] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): But?
[00:59] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): But supervisors still coordinate the remediation through phone calls and spreadsheets. So we can see the problem in three different dashboards and the actual fixing of it happens over the phone.
[01:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So it's not a visibility problem.
[01:17] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): It's absolutely not a visibility problem. We've got more visibility than we know what to do with. It's a — I don't know what you'd call it.
[01:27] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): It's a coordination problem.
[01:29] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): It's a coordination problem, yeah. Nothing moves the work along.
[01:34] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's actually a distinction I wish more people made. We see two separate things — connecting systems, which you've largely done, and operating the process on top of the connections, which is where the pain usually sits.
[01:50] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Then you've got us.
[01:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How long does a blocked installation typically sit?
[01:57] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Depends who's on. Some supervisors are brilliant and it's an hour. Others, it's two days.
[02:05] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): That variance is the actual problem, I'd say. It's not that the average is bad. It's that we can't predict it.
[02:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Do you have numbers?
[02:16] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): Some. We have outcome metrics — installations completed, first-time-fix rate, that sort of thing. Operational telemetry is weaker. We can tell you something was late. We're much worse at telling you why, or which dependency failed, or whether the same failure happened fifteen times last month.
[02:38] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That last one comes up in literally every one of these conversations.
[02:44] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): I imagine it does.
[02:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Let me try a candidate workflow and you tell me if it's the right one. An installation is blocked because equipment or permissions are missing. The system creates the appropriate remediation task, notifies regional operations, and keeps Dynamics updated as the issue changes state.
[03:08] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): [pause] That's — yeah. That's it. The last part especially.
[03:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Why the last part?
[03:16] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Because right now Dynamics goes stale the moment a human starts working the problem by phone. So the record says "blocked, awaiting equipment" and actually the equipment arrived yesterday and someone's already rescheduled it, but nobody's updated the system because they were busy fixing it.
[03:38] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And then your reporting is wrong.
[03:41] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Then everything downstream is wrong. Power BI's beautiful and it's lying.
[03:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] That's a good line.
[03:50] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): It's not mine, someone said it in a steering meeting and I've been stealing it ever since.
[03:57] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): One caveat I'd expect you to raise — what happens when it goes wrong? Missing data, an API timing out, an approver doing nothing for two days?
[04:08] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): You're asking our question for us.
[04:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather ask it than have it asked in month three.
[04:16] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): Then yes. That's exactly what we'd want to test. The happy path is not the difficult part.
[04:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And there's a specific one for you that I want to raise, because I looked at your notes. Connectivity from some field locations is intermittent, so workflows can't assume the mobile app is always online.
[04:38] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Correct. And this is the thing that kills most vendors.
[04:43] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): We had one demo where the entire premise was real-time push notifications to engineers. Which is lovely until you're in a valley in mid-Wales.
[04:55] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Or Scotland. Half our Scottish sites, you get one bar if you stand on the transformer housing.
[05:03] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please tell me nobody stands on the transformer housing.
[05:07] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): [laughs] I'm not answering that.
[05:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Right, I'm writing that down as a question for Jon rather than answering it myself. My general understanding is you'd design the workflow so the sync from the mobile app is eventual rather than assumed, and the workflow tolerates delay rather than treating it as failure. But how that's actually built is his answer, not mine.
[05:33] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): That's the right shape of answer at least.
[05:37] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Talk me through the stack.
[05:39] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Microsoft Dynamics 365. Power BI. Teams. Azure Functions. And a custom field-service mobile app that we built ourselves.
[05:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The mobile app — does it expose APIs?
[05:55] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): It does. That's my area. It's got a reasonable API surface, it's documented, it's not beautiful but it works.
[06:04] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And which of these is the system of record?
[06:08] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Dynamics for the work order. The mobile app for what actually happened on site. And those two disagree more often than I'd like.
[06:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And Power BI?
[06:21] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): Power BI is an output layer. It's not a system of record, it just reads.
[06:27] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Understood. And I'm guessing you have Power Automate.
[06:32] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): [laughs] Of course we have Power Automate.
[06:36] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Tell me honestly how it's going.
[06:39] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): We use it heavily. And we get favourable licensing on it, which matters more than I'd like it to.
[06:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): But.
[06:49] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): But complex flows are hard for operations to troubleshoot. When something breaks, it comes to my team, and my team is six people supporting two and a half thousand.
[07:02] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): And there's a knowledge problem. The people who can debug it aren't the people who understand the process.
[07:10] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): So I'm exploring alternatives. That's what this is. I want to be honest that it's exploration, not a procurement process.
[07:20] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I appreciate that and I'd rather know now.
[07:24] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): I should clarify something Carlos said, actually. About regional ownership.
[07:30] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Go on.
[07:32] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): Carlos tends to say most regions can't maintain their own automations, and that's broadly true. But two of them already have local Power Automate specialists. So the operating model isn't completely centralised today, and if we designed as though it were, those two regions would just — carry on doing their own thing.
[07:56] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): That's fair. That's a fair correction.
[08:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which two regions?
[08:02] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): North and — Carlos, is it South West or South Central?
[08:07] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): South West. [inaudible] — sorry, say again?
[08:12] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): North and South West.
[08:15] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's actually useful. Those two could be your pilot builders rather than your resistance.
[08:22] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): [pause] That's a thought.
[08:25] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): That's a better thought than I'd had, honestly.
[08:29] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's not mine originally. Most of the successful rollouts I've seen started with the people who were already building things, not the people who needed convincing.
[08:41] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Hm. Lucy, note that down.
[08:44] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): Noted.
[08:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): While we're waiting for Jon — can I ask a slightly personal question?
[08:52] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Go on.
[08:54] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Were you field originally? You talk about it like someone who's been out there.
[09:00] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Six years. Wind, mostly. I was a technician then a supervisor and then somebody made the mistake of putting me near a computer.
[09:10] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] That explains a lot.
[09:12] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): — hello? Sorry. Sorry, I'm here. Apologies, that ran over.
[09:18] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No problem. Jon, quick catch-up. Greenline are Dynamics, Power BI, Teams, Azure Functions, and a custom field-service mobile app they built themselves which exposes APIs. Power Automate incumbent, used heavily, favourable licensing. The use case is blocked installations — create remediation task, notify regional ops, keep Dynamics current as the issue changes.
[09:44] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Got it.
[09:46] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And the one I flagged for you: connectivity from some field locations is intermittent, so workflows can't assume the mobile app is online.
[09:56] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Right. That's a real design constraint and it's a good one to raise early. Can I ask a question back?
[10:04] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Please.
[10:06] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): When a device comes back online and syncs, do you get an event, or does the record just quietly change?
[10:14] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): You get an event. The app publishes on sync.
[10:19] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then you're in a much better position than most. The pattern would be that the workflow doesn't poll the device and doesn't assume presence. It reacts to the sync event when it arrives, and separately it has a timeout rule — if we haven't heard anything in N hours, that itself becomes an exception rather than a silent hang.
[10:42] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): So the not-hearing is also an event.
[10:46] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): The absence of a signal is a signal. Yes. And that's usually the bit people forget to build.
[10:53] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): We definitely haven't built that.
[10:56] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Almost nobody has, first time round.
[11:00] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): What happens to the run in the meantime? Does it just sit there?
[11:05] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Each run keeps state, so yes, it can sit in a waiting state without consuming anything or falling over. You can branch on data, pause for approvals, retry external actions, set timeout rules, and send an exception into a queue rather than failing silently.
[11:24] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Can the queue be owned by a team? Because our supervisors rotate and if it's assigned to a person, that person's on leave.
[11:34] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes. Route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. And the run history persists so you can see the inputs, which steps ran, and where it stopped.
[11:50] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): On-call is interesting for us. Field ops genuinely does run a rota.
[11:57] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then that maps well. I'd want to look at how the rota is stored, because ideally we resolve from your source of truth rather than maintaining a second copy.
[12:09] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): It's in Dynamics. Sort of.
[12:12] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): "Sort of" is doing some work in that sentence.
[12:16] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): [laughs] It's in Dynamics for some regions and in a shared calendar for others.
[12:22] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Right. So that's a thing to fix before or during, not after.
[12:28] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Add it to the list.
[12:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Jon, the big one. Dynamics.
[12:34] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yeah. So let me be straight about this because it's the thing that'll decide the evaluation. Dynamics 365 and Teams you've said are mandatory. There are integration routes to Dynamics — API-based, plus our generic REST action and webhooks. What I'm not going to tell you is that we have the deepest first-class Dynamics connector on the market, because Microsoft's own tooling will always be closer to Dynamics than we are.
[13:04] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): [pause] Right.
[13:07] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'd rather say that now than have you find it in week four.
[13:12] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): No, I — I appreciate it. But you understand that's the whole problem.
[13:18] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I do.
[13:20] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us. Power Automate is already embedded here. It's licensed, it's approved, the platform team likes it. For us to work around all of that, OrbitFlow has to be materially better, not marginally better.
[13:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the honest framing and I'm not going to argue with it. Can I ask what "materially better" would look like?
[13:50] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): [pause] Good question.
[13:53] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): Troubleshooting. If a regional supervisor can look at a failed thing and understand what happened without raising a ticket to Carlos's team, that's material.
[14:06] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Yeah. That. And reusability — if we build the remediation pattern once and use it in eight regions, rather than eight regions each building their own.
[14:19] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Both of those are things I'd want to be tested on rather than claim. The reusability one specifically — we push people hard towards small reusable subflows rather than one big canvas, and that's the mechanism. But you should make me prove it.
[14:38] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): How would we prove it?
[14:41] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Build the remediation flow for one region, then have someone from a different region adapt it for theirs, and time it. And have someone who didn't build it debug a deliberately broken run.
[14:56] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): That's a good test.
[14:59] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): That's a very good test, actually.
[15:02] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I add a slightly awkward version of it? Do the same test in Power Automate at the same time. If it's not better, you should know.
[15:13] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): You're suggesting we benchmark you against the incumbent.
[15:18] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather lose in week two than lose in month eight.
[15:23] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): [laughs] Alright.
[15:26] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): I'd have suggested it anyway.
[15:29] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I know. I'd just rather say it first.

context.text:
=== CALL-020 (call kind: cold_call)
CALL ID: CALL-020
DATE: 2026-09-30
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Kestrel Robotics
INDUSTRY: Industrial robotics
COMPANY SIZE: 150 employees
STAGE: Cold call
DURATION: 8 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Leo Grant, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Rafael Santos, COO, Kestrel Robotics
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Rafael.
[00:02] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Rafael, hi. Leo Grant, OrbitFlow. Cold call — I'll be quick and you can hang up.
[00:09] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] OrbitFlow. That's funny.
[00:13] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is it?
[00:15] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): We're three weeks into evaluating Tray.io. Your name came up on a list and got crossed off.
[00:23] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Crossed off by whom?
[00:25] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Me. About a month ago.
[00:28] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask why? Genuinely — I'm not going to argue, I just want to know.
[00:34] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Your website. It's very enterprise. Governance, compliance, workspace separation. We're a hundred and fifty people building robots. I looked at it and thought, that's not for us.
[00:49] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [pause] That's a fair read of our website.
[00:53] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You're agreeing?
[00:55] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Our marketing is aimed at companies with a governance function. You don't have one, so it isn't aimed at you.
[01:04] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): So why are you calling?
[01:06] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Because our marketing being aimed at somebody else doesn't mean the product is wrong for you. But I'd want to establish that in about four minutes rather than argue with your conclusion.
[01:19] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Go on then. Four minutes.
[01:22] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What are you trying to do with Tray?
[01:25] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Order-to-deployment. A customer orders a robot cell, and then there's engineering config, procurement of the long-lead parts, build scheduling, factory acceptance testing, shipping, and site commissioning. Seven stages, five systems, and about four months elapsed.
[01:47] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And what goes wrong?
[01:49] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Nothing goes wrong exactly. Things just take longer than they should because stage four doesn't know stage three finished until someone mentions it in a meeting.
[02:01] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How much of the four months is waiting?
[02:04] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] I don't know. That's part of why we're doing this.
[02:10] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Okay. How's the Tray evaluation going?
[02:14] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Well. Genuinely well. Their team's been good.
[02:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then I'd say two things. First, I'm not going to tell you Tray is bad. It isn't. We lose to them and we beat them and it usually comes down to fit rather than quality.
[02:32] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): What's the second?
[02:34] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Three weeks in, with a decision coming, I'd be the third horse in a two-horse race, and that's usually a waste of everyone's time.
[02:44] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You're talking yourself out of it again.
[02:47] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'm being realistic about it. Unless there's something in your evaluation that isn't going well, in which case I'd want to know what.
[02:57] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] There is one thing.
[03:00] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[03:02] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Our ERP. It's a mid-market system, quite niche in manufacturing. Tray don't have a connector and we're looking at building against its API, which our one back-end developer estimates at three weeks.
[03:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Do you believe the estimate?
[03:21] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [laughs] No.
[03:23] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Nobody ever does.
[03:25] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): It'll be six.
[03:27] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd want to be honest — there's a good chance we don't have a connector either. What's the system?
[03:34] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): I'd rather not say on a cold call, if that's alright.
[03:39] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Completely fine. Then let me answer it generally. If it's a mid-market manufacturing ERP, we probably don't have a native connector, and you'd be building against the API with our generic REST action. Which is the same three weeks. Or six.
[03:57] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): So no advantage.
[04:00] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No advantage on that specific point, no. There might be one on what happens afterwards — who maintains it, whether it's reusable across the seven stages — but that's a subtler argument and I'm not going to pretend it's decisive.
[04:17] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You keep doing this.
[04:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Doing what?
[04:21] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Conceding things.
[04:23] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather concede the things that are true and be believed on the things that aren't.
[04:29] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] Alright. What's the argument you would make?
[04:35] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Honestly, only one, and it's small. You said your one back-end developer would build the ERP integration. What happens when he's busy and someone in operations wants to change which stage triggers a notification?
[04:52] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): It waits.
[04:54] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): For how long?
[04:56] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] Depends. Weeks.
[04:59] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then the question for your evaluation — for either vendor — is whether the people who own the process can change the process without him. That's testable in a week and most evaluations don't test it.
[05:15] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): How would you test it?
[05:17] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Have someone in operations, not your developer, build one real workflow. Not with the developer sitting next to them. And see what happens.
[05:29] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] That's a good test.
[05:33] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the test that predicts whether you're happy in two years. Run it against Tray — I mean that, run it against Tray, you're three weeks in and it costs you nothing.
[05:46] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): And if they pass?
[05:48] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then buy Tray. You'll have made a good decision for a good reason.
[05:54] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [laughs] You are the strangest salesperson I've spoken to this year.
[05:59] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll take that.
[06:01] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Look — I'm not going to restart the evaluation. We've got a decision date and I'm not moving it.
[06:09] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I wouldn't ask you to.
[06:11] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): But I'll do this. Send me something short — not a deck — on how you'd approach the seven-stage thing, and specifically on the operations-can-change-it question. If we go with Tray and it doesn't work out, I'll know who to call.
[06:29] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather have that than a demo you sit through politely.
[06:34] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): When's the decision?
[06:36] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Mid-October. Fourteenth, I think, or thereabouts.
[06:42] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Would it be worth a thirty-minute call before mid-October? Not a pitch. I'd walk through how I'd structure the seven stages and you can use the thinking whichever vendor you pick.
[06:56] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): You'd do that knowing we'll probably go with Tray?
[07:01] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You're a hundred and fifty people building robots. You'll be four hundred people in three years and you'll be buying something else. I'd rather be the person who was useful.
[07:14] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] That's a long game.
[07:17] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the only game in a market this small.
[07:21] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Alright. Send the note. If it's good I'll do the thirty minutes.
[07:27] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask one thing before you go?
[07:30] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Go on.
[07:32] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The four months. Have you got a number for what a month costs you?
[07:37] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): A month of delay on a cell? Roughly, we recognise revenue on commissioning, so — a month is a month of revenue on a two hundred thousand pound order.
[07:50] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And how many orders in flight?
[07:53] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Eleven at the moment.
[07:55] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then if instrumenting the seven stages tells you where two weeks are going, that's a much bigger number than either vendor's licence.
[08:05] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [pause] That's the slide I need for my board, isn't it.
[08:10] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the slide you need regardless of who you buy from.
[08:14] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): [laughs] Send the note, Leo.
[08:17] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I will. Thanks Rafael.
[08:20] Rafael Santos (COO, Kestrel Robotics): Bye.

context.text:
=== CALL-014 (call kind: churn)
CALL ID: CALL-014
DATE: 2026-09-18
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
CUSTOMER: Verity Payments
INDUSTRY: Payments
COMPANY SIZE: 800 employees
STAGE: Churn post-mortem
DURATION: 21 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Ruth Adeyemi, Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow
- Kwame Boateng, Head of Operations, Verity Payments
- Sarah Lindqvist, Engineering Manager, Verity Payments
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Kwame, Sarah — thank you for doing this. You didn't have to.
[00:05] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): We nearly didn't, if I'm honest.
[00:08] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I know. And I want to set expectations: this isn't a save attempt. You've signed with Workato, the decision's made, and I'm not going to spend twenty minutes trying to reopen it.
[00:22] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [pause] Good. That was my concern.
[00:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What I want is to understand what went wrong properly, because two years is a long time to get something wrong and I'd like to not do it again.
[00:37] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): We'll be honest then.
[00:39] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please be.
[00:41] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I'd add — I took over this account in January, so about eight months ago. Some of what went wrong predates me and some of it doesn't, and I'd rather you told me which is which.
[00:55] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Alright. Where do you want to start?
[00:59] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): With the decision. When did you actually decide?
[01:04] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Properly? June.
[01:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): June.
[01:09] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Though I'd say the decision became inevitable in about February and it took us until June to admit it.
[01:17] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): February.
[01:19] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): February.
[01:21] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's a month after I took the account.
[01:24] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): It's not about you. I want to be clear about that.
[01:29] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I'd still like to know what happened in February.
[01:33] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): February was when we tried to build the settlement reconciliation workflow and couldn't.
[01:40] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Couldn't, or found it hard?
[01:43] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Couldn't, in the sense that the effort exceeded the value by a factor I couldn't justify to my team.
[01:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Tell me about it specifically.
[01:54] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Our settlement provider is a mid-sized European processor. You don't have a connector for them. Nobody does, to be fair — Workato doesn't either.
[02:06] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So what was the difference?
[02:09] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): The difference is that we ended up writing a custom integration either way, and once you've accepted you're writing custom integrations, you start asking what the platform is actually giving you.
[02:24] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And what was the answer?
[02:26] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Orchestration and run history, which are genuinely good. But not enough on their own for what we were paying.
[02:35] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): And this is where I'd push back on Sarah slightly.
[02:39] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Go on.
[02:41] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): The connector gap was real. But it wasn't why we left. It was the thing we pointed at.
[02:49] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What was the real reason?
[02:52] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Nobody in operations ever built anything.
[02:56] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] Say more.
[02:59] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): The entire pitch — and this is the pitch I bought, so I'm implicating myself — was that my team would own their own workflows. That we'd stop queuing behind engineering. Two years in, every single production workflow was built by Sarah's team.
[03:19] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Every one.
[03:21] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [crosstalk] So we paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. And as an engineering tool it's fine but it's not worth the premium.
[03:34] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Why didn't your team build?
[03:37] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [pause] A few reasons and none of them are flattering.
[03:42] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather have unflattering.
[03:45] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): The first workflow anyone builds is hard. Not conceptually hard — fiddly. You have to understand connections, you have to understand how data moves between steps, you have to understand what happens when something's null. My operations people are good at operations. They're not good at that, and expecting them to become good at it in their spare time was naive.
[04:11] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Did you have enablement?
[04:13] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): We had a two-day onboarding at the start. Eight people attended. Six of them never touched it again.
[04:22] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): And after that?
[04:24] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Nothing, until you arrived in January and offered some sessions.
[04:29] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Which you declined.
[04:31] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Which I declined, because by January I'd already half-concluded it wasn't going to work and I didn't want to spend my team's time on it.
[04:41] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] That's useful and it's painful.
[04:46] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): You asked.
[04:48] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I did ask. What would have changed it? If I'd arrived in month three rather than month twenty?
[04:56] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Honestly, I think if someone had sat with two of my people for a week in the first quarter and got them to ship something real, we'd still be a customer.
[05:08] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): I agree with that.
[05:10] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Not a training course. Sitting with them. Building the actual thing they needed.
[05:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): We do offer that.
[05:19] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Do you? Nobody ever offered it to me.
[05:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [pause] It's a paid professional services engagement.
[05:28] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Ah.
[05:30] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which is possibly the problem. If the thing that makes the product succeed is a paid add-on, and the customer doesn't know they need it until it's too late —
[05:41] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Then you've designed a product that fails by default for people like me.
[05:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a harsher way of putting it than I would have, but I can't argue with it.
[05:53] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Can I add the engineering perspective? Because it's different.
[05:58] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please.
[06:00] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): My team quite liked it. The run history is genuinely better than what we'd have built. The exception queues are good. When something failed at three in the morning, we could see why, and that's not nothing.
[06:16] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): So why did you support leaving?
[06:19] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Because we were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose main selling point was that we wouldn't have to maintain custom integrations. And because the licence cost was being justified by a benefit — business-user autonomy — that wasn't materialising.
[06:39] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Say the other thing.
[06:41] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): [pause] And because two of my engineers wanted to build it in-house and I spent eighteen months arguing against them, and eventually I ran out of arguments.
[06:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What was your last argument?
[06:56] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Maintenance. It's always maintenance. And it's a good argument right up until the platform also requires maintenance, at which point you're comparing two maintenance burdens and one of them costs a hundred thousand a year.
